title: Teenager loses hand picking up grenade in France school protests
summary: Nationwide protests in France over classroom conditions have disrupted lessons at hundreds of schools.
story: A 15-year-old student lost a hand on Monday picking up a police grenade as part of nationwide protests in France over classroom conditions that have disrupted lessons at hundreds of schools since last week.
Some students returned to classrooms but others maintained actions outside their schools, ahead of a day of larger demonstrations expected on Tuesday.

Authorities said the teenager was injured in the northern town of Lens. A police union source told French news agency AFP he appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police and that it exploded in his hand.

Since late September, students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of schools, complaining of teacher absences, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings ill-adapted to rising temperatures, among other grievances.
Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old protester, told CBS News his school had a rat infestation. Student leader Daphnee Die said the violence has been sparked by the students' frustration.
"It's understandable, but it's getting really dangerous, and that's why we're warning students to be safe during these events," Die told CBS News.
The unrest erupted months before elections next year that will determine the successor to centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
The government has sought to address the grievances, while accusing hard-left activists of having hijacked the protest movement.
The French Human Rights League on Monday accused security forces of using disproportionate methods against protesters, many of whom are legally minors.
"We can see that in the instructions given to the police, there is no directive to show restraint, even though they are dealing with children," league President Nathalie Tehio said.
"We're missing our lessons to give you one"
More than 400 out of France's 3,700 high schools, known as lycees, were partially or totally closed on Monday morning, the education ministry said.
A third of the 468 lycees for teenagers aged 15 to 17 were expected to be closed in the Paris region, authorities said.
In central Paris, dozens of teenage students demonstrated outside a school while passing cars honked their horns. Some classmates made their way inside to attend lessons.
"We're missing our lessons to give you one," read one cardboard sign outside the Turgot high school, located in Paris' 3rd arrondissement.
In Bordeaux, in the southwest, some students returned to the classroom while others continued to demonstrate in the presence of riot police.

Some protesters outside the Gustave Eiffel high school set off fireworks in the direction of the police, who responded sporadically with tear gas, but overall the situation remained calm, AFP reporters said.
In the northern city of Lille, masked protesters destroyed bus shelters and set fire to dustbins, as police fired tear gas toward demonstrators.
The movement started on Sept. 17 at a high school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, in support of teachers striking over a lack of staff and resources.

It gained momentum and spread across France, at times spiraling into vandalism, including the destruction of bus shelters, the burning of school entrances and clashes between protesters and security forces.
Since the start of the movement, 24 schools have been burned or ransacked, according to the education minister.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested.
Protesters have also accused the police of using excessive force, and internal investigations have been opened into at least three instances of alleged police brutality.
French leaders scramble to respond
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu set out a timetable on Sunday urging local authorities to prioritize filling gaps left by long-term teacher absences and unfilled posts.
He called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss overhauling the country's often-dilapidated school buildings.
The government is also pushing legislation to make those responsible for damaging public property pay for repairs themselves, instead of drawing on public funds.
Government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon defended the bill.

"When you have 14-, 15-, 16-year-olds who, at 9 a.m., are burning bus shelters or — perhaps even more seriously — the high school where they study, that raises the question of parental responsibility," she told the Europe1/CNews broadcaster.
Lecornu has said the draft law could allow compensation payments to be recovered from family allowances and housing benefits while preserving a minimum income threshold.
The head of the main CGT labor union, Sophie Binet, slammed what she called a "populist announcement," which she said would "end up targeting the most vulnerable families."

title: More details emerge about FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash plane
summary: Questions continue to swirl about the FlyDubai co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain and tried to crash a packed flight from Dubai to Israel.
story: Days after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about the suspect and his motive continue to swirl. He is currently being questioned in the United Arab Emirates.
Israeli investigators believe he was acting as a lone wolf, people familiar with the matter told CBS News.

The flight Wednesday, Sept. 30, from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot is currently being questioned in the United Arab Emirates. The UAE's attorney general said the suspect attacked his fellow pilot with the cockpit's emergency ax.

There were 172 people on board the plane, according to the airline. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries.
Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot?
Multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News that the co-pilot's name is Hamam al Hamami, although he has not been officially identified.

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

Buckinghamshire New University in the U.K. confirmed that al Hamami "previously completed a distance-learning course in aviation management" but did not do any pilot training there. It did not specify when he took the online course.
Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani. The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.
Netanyahu said on Oct. 4 that he has ordered a security review of international flights to Israel after the incident.
Co-pilot's motive under investigation
Details of the suspect's background and motive remain under investigation.

During his interrogation in the UAE, al Hamami said he had planned the attack even before he was employed by FlyDubai, an Israeli official told CBS News. He intended to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, the official said, adding that he had flown to Israel in the past.

The attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to sources familiar with the matter. The investigation is ongoing and all avenues are still being explored, the sources told CBS News.

"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Netanyahu said in a statement Friday, Oct. 2. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."

Netanyahu suggested to CBS News on the day of the incident, Sept. 30, that the incident looked "like a suicide attempt," referring to witnesses who said the co-pilot had tried to jam the plane's equipment instead of stabilizing the aircraft. After passengers subdued the co-pilot, he shouted for someone to kill him, Netanyahu told Fox News the following day.

In the same interview with Fox, Netanyahu said "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning had led Israel to the conclusion that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination." He did not offer more information.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz described the incident as "an attempted jihadist terror attack," and referred to the co-pilot as a "terrorist."
President Trump suggested Thursday, Oct. 1, that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
His comments went further than Netanyahu's, who told Fox it was "too early to say" if Iran was involved.

An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and were also probing whether the attacker was working alone. Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Israel was prepared to shoot the plane down, sources say

Israel was prepared to shoot down the FlyDubai plane after the captain was attacked in the cockpit, even with over 150 Israelis on board, two Israeli sources with direct knowledge of the situation told CBS News.

Israel has a long-practiced procedure for this kind of possible 9/11-style event, according to the sources. After the plane plunged 14,000 feet, the Israeli Air Force tried to contact the cockpit but got no answer. A pre-established committee was quickly roused and a command center established.

Fighter jets were scrambled and Israel's airspace was closed. But Israel called back the jets once it realized that, about 400 miles from Israel, the plane turned toward Saudi Arabia, and the Saudis scrambled their own jets.

The captain of the plane was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, according to accounts from the plane.
If Flight 1073 had gotten within a certain distance, Israel would have sent jets into Jordanian airspace to investigate, the sources told CBS News.
Co-pilot transferred to UAE for questioning

The co-pilot was placed under arrest immediately after the plane's emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu said the man was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities" and confirmed that Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."
He was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the UAE for questioning by Israeli, UAE and Saudi officials, an Israeli official confirmed to CBS News on Friday.
Netanyahu has not said what information has led investigators to conclude the co-pilot underwent radicalization.

title: Japanese leader calls woman's murder, allegedly by U.S. Marine, "heinous crime"
summary: A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine​ in Okinawa is a "heinous crime," Japan's premier said on Monday, as the new accusation of violence involving American forces sparked public outrage.
story: A woman's murder allegedly committed by a U.S. Marine in Okinawa is a "heinous crime," Japan's premier said on Monday, as the new accusation of violence involving American forces sparked public outrage.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving incidents by U.S. personnel have long sparked protests on the island, which bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of U.S. military facilities in Japan.  The new case involves Lance Cpl.     Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Futenma Air Station in Okinawa, who was arrested on suspicion of killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. He has denied the allegations, according to Japanese media.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

A patrolling police officer then found a 20-year-old man, later identified as Ballard, who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. The officer asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station, where he was arrested, NHK reported.
His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo news agency reported.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told lawmakers the government has lodged a strong protest with the United States, urging its "full cooperation with the investigation" and "strict discipline among U.S. military personnel."
"The occurrence of such a heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said.
Emotions run high
Around 100 people participated in a rally in Naha on Sunday, holding up placards stating their "strong protest" against the murder, Japanese media reported.
Okinawa native Sorane Sakihama, 24, who organized a similar rally in Tokyo on Sunday, said she cried upon learning about the woman's death.
"We couldn't protect her. That made me so angry and sad," the university student told AFP, adding that she was planning to organize another protest in front of the U.S. Embassy for Tuesday evening.
"I want to ask them — what are these soldiers stationed here for? They might say they are here to protect lives or boost security. But how can they say that when a life was taken by their own?"

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told reporters on Monday that "the government will work with the United States to thoroughly make sure there will be no recurrence, and reduce burdens on local residents."

News of the Marine's arrest immediately prompted Japan's foreign affairs and defense ministers to summon senior U.S. officials to convey their "extreme disappointment" and "lodge strong protests," Kihara said.

The incident came just a few weeks after Okinawa elected Genta Koja as its new governor, ending the eight-year rule of his predecessor, who had long pushed for a major U.S. military base to be moved off the island.
Koja, 42, accepts a central government plan to keep the U.S. Marine Corps' Futenma air base on Okinawa's main island, but to move it to a less populated location.

Calling the murder-robbery "extremely malicious in nature," Koja told reporters on Sunday it had "hugely shocked residents here who are forced to live side-by-side with the bases, and instilled new fear in them."
"I am infuriated," Koja said.
He said the incident showed U.S. efforts to "educate soldiers and improve their behavior have not been functioning at all."
Koja said he will travel to Tokyo "soon" to lodge a protest with top government officials, including Takaichi.

On Monday, U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said on social media that he is telling U.S. military commanders this week they need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." He also said that he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Today it hosts 70% of America's military facilities and most of the 50,000 U.S. troops based in Japan.

There has been anger over increasing crime linked to the U.S. military on the island. The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to prefectural police.
A Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison last year.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
Under a bilateral status of forces agreement, the case is being handled by the Japanese authorities because the suspect was not on duty and was arrested off base.
Japanese prosecutors started examining the suspect's case on Monday to determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, he could face life in prison or the death penalty.

title: U.S. Marine arrested, accused of killing Japanese woman in Okinawa
summary: U.S. authorities in Japan acknowledged that a U.S. service member was in police custody and pledged to fully cooperate with the investigation.
story: A U.S. Marine stationed in Japan's southern island of Okinawa was arrested following the death of a Japanese woman, local police said on Sunday. Japan lodged a strong protest with the U.S. and demanded maximum cooperation with the investigation.

Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, Okinawa prefectural police said. Ballard denied the allegations, police said.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Ballard was arrested when a patrolling officer saw him walking later Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and arm tattoos matched those of the man in security footage, Kyodo News Agency reported.

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," newly elected Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters, the Associated Press reported. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."

"We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened. My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter," the woman's brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper.

The U.S. Embassy in Tokyo said it was aware that a U.S. service member was in police custody following the death of a Japanese national in Okinawa and that they are "communicating and cooperating" with Japanese authorities amid the investigation.
"We extend our sincere condolences to the victim's family," the embassy said on social media.

George Glass, the U.S. Ambassador to Japan, said on social media that he has spoken with Japan's foreign ministry and Okinawa's governor, offering "our sincere condolences and pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues."

On Monday, Glass said he is telling U.S. military commanders of the need "to hold our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity." Glass said he and Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, discussed the "next steps in strengthening that bond of trust with our Japanese partners and base-hosting communities."
The latest case comes as Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's Cabinet pushes to further fortify its Japanese military presence on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military.
Takaichi said Japan had lodged a protest with U.S. authorities and called the crime "exceptionally brutal and vicious."
"The occurrence of the heinous crime is extremely regrettable," Takaichi said in her message on social media.

She said Tokyo has urged the U.S. to "provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among U.S. military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes."
The U.S. Marine Corps said it is fully cooperating with Japanese authorities.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior," the statement said.
The U.S. has around 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa, which the U.S. held from the end of World War II until 1972.

Crimes, including rapes, assaults and drunk-driving accidents committed by U.S. personnel have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. The number of arrests related to U.S. service members and their families exceeded 100 last year, according to prefectural police.
"Incidents and accidents involving U.S. military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen," Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
Last year, a Japanese court sentenced a U.S. Marine accused of choking and attempting to rape a woman in her 20s to seven years in prison.
In 2017, a former U.S. Marine and civilian military base worker was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, U.S. Forces Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated U.S. Marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.

title: Ex-Prince Andrew challenges validity of Epstein-related search warrants
summary: Britain's former Prince Andrew is challenging the validity of search warrants issued for his homes prior to his arrest over his dealings with Jeffrey Epstein.
story: London — Disgraced former Prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched a legal challenge over search warrants for his royal homes that were issued before his February arrest, Britain's judiciary confirmed Monday.

The judiciary confirmed that the U.K. High Court was to hold a private hearing on Thursday, as King Charles III's brother challenges Thames Valley Police over the searches carried out in Windsor, west of London, and Sandringham, in eastern England.
The force arrested Andrew on his 66th birthday on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office, related to his links to the late U.S. sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Andrew was released the same day after hours of police questioning, but remained under investigation. He has denied all wrongdoing in his associations with the disgraced American financier.
His shock arrest prompted Charles to issue a statement insisting "the law must take its course."

The Daily Telegraph reported the legal challenge late on Sunday. The newspaper noted it was the first time a member of Britain's royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
It said Andrew's legal team wanted to examine whether the search warrants granted by a judge at London's Old Bailey court — formally known as the Central Criminal Court —   were lawful.
Andrew's legal team did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment.
Andrew's effort to have court "quash search warrants"

The judiciary's press office said "the case concerns an application by Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor for a judicial review to quash search warrants issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February 2026."
If the review were to throw out the warrants, it would potentially deprive prosecutors handling the case of any evidence discovered during the searches of the former prince's homes.

Andrew's arrest and the police searches marked a new low for the royal, who was stripped of his royal titles last year and ousted from his Windsor home over his Epstein connections. The government has even mulled passing a law to remove him from the royal line of succession.

Scandal has engulfed the king's younger brother since one of Epstein's accusers, Virginia Giuffre, claimed in her posthumous memoirs that she had been trafficked three times to have sex with Andrew when she was a teenager. Giuffre died last year by suicide at the age of 41.
The former prince has repeatedly denied the claims. He settled a U.S. civil lawsuit in 2022 brought by Giuffre while not admitting liability.

The Thames Valley Police probe follows new revelations from documents relating to the American financier released by the United States earlier this year, including emails in which Andrew appeared to share potentially confidential information with him.
"Investigation into misconduct in public office continues"

In one November 2010 email released by the U.S. government, Andrew appeared to share with the U.S. financier reports on his visit to several Asian countries. Two years earlier, Epstein had been convicted in the United States of procuring a child for prostitution.

At least nine British police forces confirmed they were looking into claims — some related to Andrew — stemming from the batch of some 3 million Epstein files released by the U.S. authorities in January.

However, the Thames Valley investigation appears to be the most advanced. Its officers, who swooped on the remote Sandringham royal estate in eastern England to detain Andrew, searched his home there and his former Royal Lodge residence in Windsor, west of London.
The raid in Windsor lasted six days.
In response to Andrew's legal challenge, Thames Valley Police said in a statement that its "investigation into misconduct in public office continues."
"We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained," it added. "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."

title: Extreme heat putting births in jeopardy, U.N. climate chief warns
summary: Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the U.N. climate chief is warning.
story: Nadi, Fiji — Extreme heat is increasingly linked to problems such as premature births or underweight babies, the U.N. climate chief warned on Monday as Fiji hosted talks ahead of a major summit.
This week's meetings in the city of Nadi and on the atoll nation of Tuvalu are aimed at drawing the world's attention to life on the front line of climate change in the Pacific.
They are a precursor to the larger U.N.-sponsored global climate summit, known as COP31, to be held in Turkey next month.

Highlighting the need for urgent action, United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell cited a new survey showing more than two-thirds of health professionals across five continents had seen complications caused by intense heat in the past five years.
"Climate-driven extreme heat during pregnancy is increasingly linked to premature birth, stillbirth, low birth weight, and maternal complications," he said.

The Plan International charity said in a separate report on Monday that climate disasters were also increasing the risk of child marriage and teen pregnancies, in part through their impact on the health and education services on which girls depend.
The South Pacific is among the most vulnerable regions in the world to global warming — from rising sea waters jeopardizing homes to increasing temperatures causing coral bleaching.
Fiji's climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, called for commitments from developing nations to a "just transition" with support for "countries in the world that suffer the most."
A U.N. report released in August found developing countries needed $310 billion to $365 billion to adapt, yet had only $26 billion in adaptation finance available in 2023.
"We rely on and we appeal to countries to commit to climate finance," Tabuya said.

Australia — the head of this year's climate negotiations and a major coal exporter— faces accusations of hypocrisy: Its sales of the fossil fuel have boomed on the back of demand caused by the Middle East conflict.
Tabuya told journalists there had been "frank discussion" on Monday with her Australian counterpart Chris Bowen and Pacific officials.
"Yes, we have sentiments expressed from certain countries," she said, when asked if she backed calls from other Pacific leaders for Australia to halt expansion of coal and gas projects.
"But for the Pacific, it's important at this pre-COP that we find common ground. There will be things that we disagree on, but we can agree to disagree," Tabuya said.
Refocusing on limiting global warming

Also high on the agenda is a push by Pacific leaders for the world to stick to a target of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a threshhold that was breached in 2025 — and give more attention to the impact on oceans.
"Keeping 1.5 alive means hope — hope for Tuvalu, hope for Kiribati, hope for small island atolls around the world," Bowen told journalists.
"We can actually come to this conversation and say, 'as a fossil-fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table,'" he said.

Sea levels are also rising at a record pace, driven by warming oceans and glacier melt, according to the August U.N. report.  .Up to 1.2 billion people could be displaced by 2050, with Pacific island countries experiencing sea level rise at twice the global average, it said.
Regional leaders have pitched the pre-COP as a chance to bring the world to the Pacific, and they are keen to show the impact climate change is having on the region.
In Naidiri Village, a marine protected area an hour's drive south of Nadi, locals described efforts to combat coral bleaching and improve ocean health.
"Countries that don't cause climate change are being affected," Joseva Kunagado, 21, told AFP.

Manoa Duwai, who set up Naidiri Village's marine protected area more than a decade ago after realizing what the damage wrought by overfishing is, said they were experiencing climate change "every day."
"The sea level is rising, and a heat wave earlier this year," he said. "A message to the developed countries: Do remember, don't forget."
Delegates will also take a one-day trip on Tuesday to low-lying Tuvalu, which is already laying plans to relocate its population if it's consumed by the ocean.
Tuvalu is one of the world's least visited countries and the highest point in its capital, Funafuti, is just 6.6 feet above sea level.

title: Cat-stealing ring that took 2,700 pets for food busted by police
summary: Fur removal machines, cat traps and measuring scales were among items confiscated during investigations into the alleged cat-stealing ring.
story: Vietnamese police have arrested 12 men accused of stealing nearly 2,700 cats during night raids into residential neighborhoods, taking the pets to be slaughtered for food, police and state media said on Monday.
Fur removal machines, cat traps and measuring scales were among items confiscated during investigations into the alleged cat-stealing ring in Ho Chi Minh City.
Consumption of dogs and cats is legal in Vietnam, where many restaurants openly advertise the meat, but vendors are required to obtain certificates showing the origin of the animals.
Media reports have said that stolen cats can be sold at restaurants for at least 70,000 dong ($2.70) per kilogram.
The 12 men were arrested on allegations of property theft and admitted "to stealing and trafficking approximately 2,700 cats of various types," police said in a statement.
Criminal proceedings began on Sunday, but it was not clear when the men were detained.

The suspects split into small groups and traveled by motorbike to residential neighborhoods to look for cats, the state-owned Tuoi Tre newspaper reported. The suspects mainly operated from 11:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m., the outlet reported.
The network was first discovered in July, with police seizing 50 live cats alongside 55 cat traps, two scales and two fur removal machines.
Each team was estimated to have stolen between four and 10 cats per night.

Police in Ho Chi Minh City arrested 18 people earlier this year accused of being part of two separate cat-stealing rings. In June, police rescued more than 400 cats in a major bust of a cat meat crime ring in Ho Chi Minh City, and at least 40 were reunited with their owners. However, several of the cats died because of the harsh conditions they were found in, animal welfare groups said.

"It was quite an overwhelming sight to see so many cats seized from just a single transport in Vietnam's illicit cat meat trade," said Phuong Tham, Humane World for Animals Viet Nam country director, in a statement at the time. "The sad truth about this trade is that thousands of cats every month are being stolen, trafficked and slaughtered for meat across the country, and the fate of most is to end up at a slaughterhouse or restaurant to be killed and eaten."

title: Another U.S. strike on alleged drug-smuggling boat kills 4, SOUTHCOM says
summary: The U.S. military said it attacked a boat suspected of smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its yearlong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.
story: The U.S. military said it attacked a boat suspected of being used to smuggle drugs in the Caribbean Sea on Sunday, killing four people, as the Trump administration continues its yearlong campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America.

The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed in boat strikes by the U.S. military to at least 235 in 70 strikes since the administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025. As with most of the military's statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, the U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes.

The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed what appeared to be an explosion destroying a moving boat, which the military said was a go-fast vessel.

On October 4, under the direction of #SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in… pic.twitter.com/aK0jCTl74o

The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said during a visit to Panama in August that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow the U.S. to carry out joint military operations against criminal groups on their soil. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.

President Trump has said the U.S. is in "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the U.S. and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

title: Brazil presidential election heads to runoff after no majority vote
summary: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump and the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, and Brazil's veteran President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff on Oct. 25.
story: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, and Brazil's veteran President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff on Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America's powerhouse economy.

The country's electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the more than 50% of the total vote needed for an outright win.
Brazil's electoral court in Brasilia had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula's 53.7 million, with 99.8% of the vote reported.
Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house.
"Brazil wants change, that's the reading of what happened today," Bolsonaro said. "It's the end of the Workers' Party era," he added, in a reference to Lula's party.
Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was "unexpected" as he had thought he could win in the first round.
"Tomorrow we start a new campaign," Lula said. "I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan."

Trump allies have fared well in recent elections in Latin America, including in Argentina, Colombia, Honduras and Peru. Lula has accused the U.S. administration of trying to sway his country's election to Bolsonaro by imposing tariffs, revoking the visa of the country's ambassador to Washington, and imposing sanctions on government officials and one Supreme Court justice.
The Trump administration did not respond to a request for comment on whether it is seeking to interfere in the vote.

The next presidential term begins on Jan. 5, 2027. The winner will be in charge of Latin America's biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China.
Lula faces a tough battle

Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who found moderate support in Sunday's election, have previously said they will not endorse either bidder in the runoff.
With another 21 days of campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival's many legal woes.

While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians' lives.
But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.
Sen. Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals.

He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics.
"Brazil needs change. Brazil can't stand so much suffering," he told reporters at the Rio de Janeiro voting center, where he cast his vote Sunday.
Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil's population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula's Workers Party, according to multiple polls.
Four years ago, Lula beat the then-incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes.
Voters choose between incumbent or return to right

"I'm feeling calm but very sad with the result," said Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro who watched the count with friends at a bar. "I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win."

Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro's eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father's footsteps.
"I voted for his father, and I don't regret it," she said.

The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father's presidency, "people felt more at ease to discriminate," she said.
"I'm an LGBTQ+ woman, I can't think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected," she added.
Rosângela Resende da Rocha, a 69-year-old who was previously a stay-at-home mom, said she supported Lula's social policies that help the "less fortunate" and how he stands up to Mr. Trump.
"That crazy guy wants to come in here to buy our country, so that our country will be like it is over there," she said at a voting center in Brasilia. "He won't succeed if Lula wins."
Confidence in Brazil's electronic voting system
No significant fraud has ever been detected since Brazil adopted its electronic voting system in the 1990s.

The Organization of American States' electoral observation mission reported Sunday that "the voting has been going smoothly and under adequate safety conditions." Electoral authorities have assured that electronic votes are secure and verifiable.

"We are almost three hours away from the end of the voting and everything is proceeding normally and with the greatest possible transparency," the president of the Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, said Sunday afternoon, adding that there was "no concrete indication of international interference."
Voters appeared largely confident that the country's voting system can't be tampered with.
Josemar Lauriano Pereira, a 46-year-old lawyer in Rio de Janeiro, said that the rapid availability of results helped combat fraud and uncertainty.
"When results take a lot of time, it creates an opening for people to cast doubt on the results, to say there's been a problem," he said.

title: FlyDubai co-pilot was likely lone wolf, Israeli investigators believe
summary: The FlyDubai​ alleged attempted hijacking was likely a lone wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to people familiar with the matter.
story: The FlyDubai alleged attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to people familiar with the matter.
The investigation is still in full swing and all avenues are still being explored, the people familiar told CBS News.

The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.

The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

The co-pilot is currently in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing a second round of interrogation after first being questioned by Saudi authorities when the plane made its emergency landing. Israel has sent its own representatives to the UAE to participate in the investigation.
President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Netanyahu told CBS News on Wednesday that the co-pilot's motives are still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, adding, "I think it looks like a suicide attempt."

Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.
The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

title: FBI arrests woman at LAX accused of being Chinese agent
summary: Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was arrested on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
story: The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.

Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.

A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.

Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.

"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.

Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades. It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.

The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.

Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.

Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA, Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.

Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang, 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.

The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.

New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.

In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

title: Key Biden aide recalls "draconian measures" being considered against Israel
summary: In a CBS News interview, Biden-era Middle East adviser Brett McGurk recounted the administration's response to the Oct. 7 attack, its handling of the Israel-Hamas war, the role of Iran and the long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
story: President Joe Biden was on the verge of taking "draconian measures" after an Israeli military drone strike killed seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in the Gaza Strip in April 2024, but U.S. intelligence that Iran was about to launch an "unprecedented" aerial attack on Israel prevented Biden from moving forward, according to Brett McGurk, a top Middle East adviser to four presidents.
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" taped Thursday, McGurk described Biden as "fed up" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war in Gaza.

"At that moment, if not for that impending missile attack, which we then had to deploy military forces … I think we would have taken some pretty draconian measures against Israel," he said, adding that cutting off U.S. weapons to Israel "was very much on the table."

The U.S. and its Arab and European partners helped protect Israel from the Iranian attack, which McGurk said included 120 ballistic missiles, 170 drones and 30 cruise missiles that were "all launched to land at the same time."

In his new memoir titled "Brink," which is set to be published Tuesday, McGurk recalled a tense conversation between Biden and Netanyahu around that time in which the U.S. leader warned the prime minister he could end the weapons supply. At the time, the Israeli government said it believed there were more than 130 hostages in Gaza and around 34,000 Gazan deaths, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Ministry of Health.
"You think I'm Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal," McGurk quotes Biden as saying.
McGurk spoke to CBS News ahead of the release of his new book on the Gaza hostage negotiations, "Brink."

The longtime foreign policy aide recounted the Biden administration's initial reaction to Hamas' Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel, its handling of Israel's war against Hamas in Gaza, the efforts to secure an Israel-Hamas ceasefire and hostage release deal, the role of Iran and — starting years earlier — a long-sought push to normalize relations between Israel and Saudi Arabia.
McGurk is no longer working with the Bidens and is currently a CNN contributor.
McGurk: "If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis"

Biden's handling of the Israel-Hamas war has drawn years of scrutiny — including from within his own party. During the 2024 presidential campaign, the administration faced intense pressure to stop military aid to Israel amid the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

The U.S. is the largest weapons supplier to Israel, and provides billions in aid. A 2023 State Department review of Israel's conduct found that it was "reasonable to assess" that Israeli security forces have used U.S.-made weapons in ways "inconsistent with" international humanitarian law obligations. Casualties in Gaza, "including high levels of civilian casualties," raised "substantial questions as to whether the IDF is using" U.S.-made weapons "effectively in all cases," the report said.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen told "Face the Nation" in November 2024 that Biden didn't use U.S. leverage effectively, arguing he sent Israel "more bombs and more money" after Netaynahu disregarded his requests, and pointed to U.S. laws blocking arms shipments to military units that violated human rights.

Since then, debates over the future of U.S.-Israel relations have continued to rage. Some of the criticism that the Biden administration was not strong enough in its response to Israeli actions in Gaza has been directed at McGurk, who was the White House National Security Council's coordinator for the Middle East and North Africa and one of his most influential advisers.

McGurk noted that the Biden administration did pause some weapons transfers to Israel, including 2,000-pound bombs but never instituted a weapons halt. He believes some of the calls to go further may not have been effective.

"Israel also has one of the largest arms industries in the world, so the idea that had Biden gone further on a step on that course, it would have stopped the war, I just think the record does not support that," McGurk said.
McGurk also argued that exerting too much public pressure on Israel could have hardened Hamas' stance, ultimately setting back the negotiations to end the war in Gaza and release the hostages.

"I come back to the question: How do you end this crisis?" he said. "And I think the record shows: If you just stop American support for Israel, that is not going to end the crisis, it's going to make it worse."

At the same time as the Israel-Hamas war, attacks on U.S. forces by Iranian-backed proxy groups surged. McGurk pushed Biden to punish Iran in an effort to deter the attacks, and expressed some frustration with Biden administration colleagues who were wary of striking Iranian officials in response.
What would've happened if Iran "made a dash" toward weapons-grade uranium
McGurk said part of Biden's goal was to prevent the outbreak of a broader regional war. Meanwhile, periodic aerial attacks between Iran and Israel continued.
In December 2024, McGurk traveled to Israel with national security adviser Jake Sullivan as they worked toward a deal with Hamas to release the remaining Israeli hostages.

During the visit, according to McGurk, Netanyahu talked about taking out nuclear sites in Iran, including at Fordow, a facility built inside a mountain that processed and stored highly enriched uranium. Fordow was one of the three Iranian nuclear sites that President Trump ordered to be bombed  in June 2025, eight months before the Trump administration and Israeli forces launched a wider war against Iran.

McGurk said the Biden administration was concerned in late 2024 that Iran "might make a dash" toward making weapons-grade uranium, and officials were open to carrying out strikes if there were evidence obtained that showed Iran was making a bomb. Netanyahu urged the US not to wait for that step. Iran had been building up a stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, which is a short step from the material required to build a bomb.

"We actually had a principals committee meeting — that's everybody around the table — what would we do if we see that?" McGurk said. "And as I recall, unanimity on: We would do the strike in Fordow. We didn't see that. We sent a message to Iran, don't even think about it. But yet Netanyahu was clearly contemplating that."

Hamas and Israel struck a ceasefire deal that led to the release of some hostages a month after that, just days before President Trump was inaugurated and the Biden national security team left the White House. McGurk said he and Mr. Trump's Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff "agreed we're going to work in lockstep." He described how the Biden and Trump teams put pressure on both Hamas and Israel.
Hamas released the last living hostages in October 2025, as part of another ceasefire agreement.
U.S. saw no "warning or indicator" of Oct. 7 attack

The circumstances leading up to the Oct. 7 attack have drawn renewed attention in recent weeks, as The New York Times, The Atlantic and the Israeli newspaper Haaretz report on warnings that officials in Egypt and the United Arab Emirates allegedly delivered to Israel that Hamas was planning a major attack. Netanyahu has strongly denied that there were any warnings, but his opponents in Israel's election later this month have expressed outrage.

CBS has confirmed via a former US official and a diplomatic source that Emirati Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed al Nahyan, President of the UAE, did share a warning with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu in the weeks leading up to the attack. The UAE had learned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major attack but did not have specific intelligence such as a date, time or location.
McGurk told CBS News the U.S. had no intelligence that could have warned about Hamas' Oct. 7 attack.
"We did not have anything in our system that would have been a warning and indicator," he said. "No U.S. intelligence of a warning or indicator."
But he said Israel should launch an official inquiry that probes its own security establishment and political leadership, much like the U.S. did after the 9/11 attacks.

"I think they had an assumption that was deeply ingrained that Hamas was deterred, assuaged, and was not about to do something massive on any scale like this," McGurk said. "I think that was a false assumption in their system, a failure of imagination, and it was tragic."
McGurk on the Biden-MBS fist bump: "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand"

Hours before the Oct. 7 2023 attack, McGurk said he met with the Saudi Arabian Ambassador to the U.S., Princess Reema Bandar,  to discuss a different issue — a potential pathway for Israel and Saudi Arabia to normalize relations.

MB SUGGESTIONED INSERT: Just weeks prior, Prime Minister Netanyahu had stood at the UN General Assembly in New York and predicted a new Middle East to include normalization between the Jewish State and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, birthplace of Islam.
"I believe that we are at the cusp of an even more dramatic breakthrough: an historic peace with Saudi Arabia," Netanyahu said.

The idea of Saudi Arabia establishing formal diplomatic ties with Israel had been floated to McGurk by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman nearly two years earlier, in January 2021, shortly after Biden took office, McGurk said, a deal that would have included a pathway to a Palestinian peace agreement. McGurk said he reported that extraordinary offer back to the President, but the U.S. did not act on it.

Biden was skeptical of Saudi Arabia, vowing in the 2020 Democratic primaries to treat the kingdom as a "pariah" due to U.S. intelligence indicating that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was linked to the murder of Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

McGurk also explained that Biden did not want to focus on the Middle East, and only reached out to the Gulf States after the chaotic August 2021 U.S. exit from Afghanistan caused the emergency need for the U.S. to ask those governments to take in Afghan allies fleeing the Taliban. The U.S. needed another favor in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, and turned again to the Gulf states, specifically Saudi Arabia, asking them to pump more oil to alleviate a spike in prices.

Rebuilding frayed relations because a necessity for U.S. national security. McGurk said it was a "mistake" that administration officials did not engage with Saudi Arabia more frequently early in Biden's term. He convinced him to visit in 2022.

McGurk offered rare criticism of Biden over his 2022 visit to Saudi Arabia, which came during a global spike in energy prices. He recounts that for 18 minutes Air Force One sat on the tarmac in the Kingdom as Biden argued with aides over how he would greet the Crown Price at his palace.
Rather than shaking bin Salman's hand, Biden famously gave him a fist bump.

"He was concerned about the optics and the imagery," McGurk told CBS News, and "I encouraged the president to just shake his hand." He later said: "We were asking some very hard things to the Saudis that we needed for our core interests, and so I think the fist bump set us back."

By 2023, the U.S., Israel and Saudi Arabia were working toward a normalization agreement, a complicated deal that likely would have involved the U.S. offering Saudi Arabia a civil nuclear program and Israel agreeing to concessions around the Palestinian territories. The Oct. 7 attack derailed those talks — and President Biden often openly theorized that Hamas may have sought to prevent normalization.
McGurk said he "never saw anything to tie a direct connection," but didn't rule out that idea.

"Hamas, of course, does not recognize Israel, wants to destroy Israel, and I would not be surprised if one of the motivations on October 7th was to knock this agenda off the table," McGurk said, calling the prospect of Saudi-Israeli normalization "one of the biggest deals since the Cold War."

President Trump has revived the terms of that U.S.-Saudi arrangement, including the pledge to develop a civil nuclear program. However, the current Israel government has refused to discuss a Palestinian state in the wake of Oct 7 attacks, and the civilian death toll in Gaza from the war makes normalization more politically difficult for Saudi leaders.

title: Hero passenger on FlyDubai flight: "We are going to survive"
summary: "Sunday Morning" talked with passengers who heroically helped avert disaster this past Wednesday by subduing the co-pilot attempting to crash their Boeing 737 Max into the Arabian Desert.
story: This past Wednesday, they were strangers on a plane. By Friday, they were family. It was the first time hero passengers Daniel Schlichter, Zvika Manes, Tal Samuel and Asaf Rajuan had seen each other since those terrifying moments on FlyDubai's Flight 1073.

"That minute is probably the longest minute of my life," said Schlichter about the plane's terrifying freefall. "And the first thing that went up is actually 9/11. And I said, 'How can it be? How can we end this life like that?' You see all your life and you think about what is important. And just holding my wife's hand and saying, 'If we have to go, we have to go.'"

Their Boeing 737 Max was nosediving into the Arabian Desert nearly at the speed of sound. The co-pilot from Oman had stabbed the captain, grabbed the controls, and tried to crash the plane full of Israeli passengers. The jet plummeted 14,000 feet in seconds. They were less than 30 seconds from crashing, with G-forces Manes described as being "like a roller coaster."

What they couldn't have known was that inside the locked cockpit, Captain Smit Machchhar was fighting for his life, as he told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday: "The co-pilot, he wanted to pray. And suddenly there was a big blow to the back of my head," Machchhar said. "I did try to stop him, and that's when I gave everything that I had, and just went for the door and opened the door and thankfully people were waiting."

Manes and his family were sitting in the first row. His wife had just taken his daughter to the bathroom. "I heard my daughter shouting, 'He's stabbing the pilot. He's stabbing the pilot.' She was shouting like animal," he said.
At that moment, Rajuan said they thought they were going to die.
Schlichter, holding his wife's hand, thought to himself, "'If I have to go, I'll hold her hand as tight as possible, and we'll go together.' That's it."
Almost simultaneously, these passengers decided they had to take action.

"I saw my daughter and my wife, and I understand that I must run. I turn, switch to an animal switch, and I feel really like an animal. … I decided that we are going to survive, try to survive, to save my family," Manes said.

Tal Samuel said, "Everyone here, on the day-to-day, are super decent and polite people. But when you watch the situation, you didn't see a finance person, and you didn't see an insurance guy. It was something different. It was like lions that are in a killing mode."
Along with an Israeli plumber named Yaniv Hayoun, they ran toward the bleeding captain, whom they called a hero.
"Not just because he opened the door. Because he had amazing fight with the terrorist. He really fight him," said Rajuan.

Then, they piled onto the co-pilot, Hamam al Hamami, who we've now learned had been banned from flying in his home country, Oman, because of concerns he'd adopted extremist views. And Israeli investigators say they've uncovered social media posts where he talked about killing Jews. Officials in the United Arab Emirates now say he'd committed a "terrorist act."
"I was jumping on him, punching," said Manes. "He tried to resist, and we didn't know if he has a knife."
With a pack of men struggling at the entrance to the cockpit, just then, Tal Samuel looked up and saw the cockpit was empty. He remembered he had been sitting next to two off-duty pilots.
"And the other pilot that came from his seat, because they are blocking the entrance to the cockpit, so that's why he jumped," Samuel said.
According to Rajuan, the pilot leaned over the chair to grab the controls and right the plane.
They were out of freefall. But the captain was bleeding out. "And we are shouting, if there is a doctor in the plane," Manes said.
Shota Musaev, a dentist, said to his wife, "'I need to go,' and, 'I love you.' That's it."
Musaev got up and began treating stab wounds on Machchhar's head and hands. Musaev was afraid he could die from the wounds.
"Yes, I think we have not more time. I check everything, of course, I said to the steward, 'We have no time – land the plane,'" he said.
But the nearest airport was in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, a country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel.
"I was worried that maybe they will arrest us," Manes said, "because they will see blood all over."
But they were not arrested — they were welcomed.

The captain was whisked to a hospital where he's recovering, but at night Dr. Musaev remains with his heroic patient. He said that he can see his face when he closes his eyes: "Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. I think from this time we are a very big family, you know."
And then, in Hebrew, Musaev said, "If he hadn't been smart and heroic, we would not be alive. On the other hand, if we had not been heroes, he would not be alive."
Produced by Sari Aviv, Jon Carras and Christine Romo. Editors: Chad Cardin and George Pozderec.

FlyDubai

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Former Prince Andrew isn't waiting quietly for the police investigation into him to play out.
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor launched a legal challenge over searches of his homes following his February arrest.

Mountbatten-Windsor asked the court to rule on whether Thames Valley Police lawfully searched his homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate, according to The Daily Telegraph. A hearing will be held Thursday.
PRINCE WILLIAM SEES DISGRACED ANDREW AS ‘A TROUBLED SOUL’ BUT EPSTEIN FALLOUT LEAVES ‘NO COMING BACK’: AUTHOR
Former Prince Andrew launched a legal challenge questioning whether police lawfully searched his royal residences following his February arrest. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."
Fox News Digital reached out to Andrew's attorney for comment.
The legal challenge could have significant consequences for the investigation, particularly if the court finds fault with how police obtained evidence.

"He is fighting the police process rather than waiting for the investigation to conclude," Richard Fitzwilliams, royal commentator, told Fox News Digital. "If he wins, it might affect evidence obtained through the searches which he is claiming were not lawfully conducted."

"The background to this is that the police have reportedly not obtained access to the unredacted Epstein files, which has reportedly affected their ability to investigate links between Andrew and Epstein," Fitzwilliams added. title: Prince William ‘incandescent with anger’ at Prince Harry as Diana anniversary deepens royal rift: Piers Morgan
summary: Piers Morgan says Prince William is "incandescent with anger" over Prince Harry's attacks on the royal family, making a Diana documentary reunion unlikely.
story: Piers Morgan explains why he sympathizes with Prince William amid his ongoing estrangement from younger brother Prince Harry.

Prince William isn't expected to reunite with his brother, Prince Harry, for a potential new documentary about their late mother. Asked about the reports, Piers Morgan argued the brothers' long-running rift makes any reunion unlikely.
"Well, they don't speak to each other and haven't done so for years," the host of "Piers Morgan Uncensored" told Fox News Digital.

Morgan went on to say that William is "absolutely incandescent with anger about what his little brother did in trashing the royal family," including "writing books, doing Netflix documentary shows, doing podcasts, always dumping on the family and attacking his wife, Catherine, attacking Camilla, attacking King Charles."
PRINCE WILLIAM'S DOOR IS 'BOLTED SHUT' AS PRINCE HARRY PLANS UK RETURN WITH MEGHAN MARKLE, CHILDREN: EXPERT

Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital Prince William (left) and Prince Harry (right) haven't been on speaking terms since 2022 following the death of Queen Elizabeth II. (Kirsty O'Connor - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"Harry took out the spray gun," said Morgan. "And when you do that, then family members who are on the receiving end aren't going to like it. My sympathies are entirely with Prince William, who's a thoroughly honorable, decent young man who's just had it with his brother and wants nothing to do with him."
Fox News Digital reached out to Kensington Palace for comment.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a visit to Southport Community Centre in Southport, England, on Oct. 10, 2024. (Getty Images)

Morgan has been outspoken about Harry and Meghan over the years, taking issue with their decision to step back from royal duties, their media projects and their public comments about life within the royal family.

Several royal experts previously told Fox News Digital that the brothers haven't been on speaking terms since 2022.

Diana, Princess of Wales, leaves the British Lung Foundation in Hatton Garden after being presented with a bouquet of the first rose named after her. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
The Times also reported that William views his tributes marking Diana's 20th anniversary as his public "catharsis."

Prince Harry (left) and Prince William (right) attend the unveiling of a statue of their mother, Princess Diana, at The Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace, London on July 1, 2021, which would have been her 60th birthday. (Dominic Lipinski/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Prince Harry is considering several projects to mark the 30th anniversary of Diana's death, People magazine reported. According to the outlet, the Duke of Sussex has been exploring how he can "most meaningfully" honor his mother and her legacy ahead of the milestone on Aug. 31, 2027.

While various ideas are under discussion, People reported that no documentary has been finalized or confirmed. Harry has reached out to family members and friends connected to his late mother, multiple sources told the outlet.
Princess Diana receives a warm welcome from crowds in Argentina at the start of her visit. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Archewell for comment.

Turner said the estrangement between the brothers has reportedly left their father, King Charles III, "scratching his head."
Prince Charles and Princess Diana ride in a carriage on their wedding day. (WireImage)
"His two sons appear to be as distant as ever," said Turner. "Perhaps this is Charles' personal annus horribilis."
Prince William and Prince Harry look at floral tributes to Diana, Princess of Wales, outside Kensington Palace in London, England, on Sept. 5, 1997. (WireImage)
Friends of William told The Times that next year is "a difficult situation for him" and that he remains "really emotional" about his mother's death.

The Times also reported that William had found his uncle Charles Spencer's newly published memoir, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," "difficult," after receiving little advance warning about the book. The book, about Diana, is highly critical of King Charles III, who is receiving treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer.

Copies of Charles Spencer's book about his sister, Diana, Princess of Wales, are displayed on its publication day at Foyles on Charing Cross Road in London, England, on Sept. 22, 2026. The book, "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister," recounts Earl Spencer's childhood with Diana. (In Pictures via Getty Images)

Turner wondered whether William had initially considered a project about his mother but scrapped the idea following the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's return to the U.K. in August. Turner suggested that William stepping aside could make it less likely that competing projects would pit the brothers against each other.

Prince William (pictured here) did not meet with his estranged younger brother, Prince Harry, who spent time with their father, King Charles III, at Highgrove House, the monarch's private residence, on July 10, 2026. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"William and Catherine have seemed to have increased their number of public events which, not surprisingly, have been well documented," he said.

William was 15 when Diana died. Harry was 12. Over the years, Harry has spoken publicly about how Diana's death has deeply affected him. In his 2023 memoir, "Spare," Harry recalled breaking down as Diana was buried at Althorp, her ancestral home.

"It was reported that Mummy's hands were folded across her chest and between them was placed a photo of me and Willy, possibly the only two men who ever truly loved her," he wrote, as quoted by People magazine. "Certainly, the two who loved her most."
Diana, Princess of Wales, died in 1997. She was 36. (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Engelbert Humperdinck is reflecting on the dark side of trying to make it in the music industry, claiming he was repeatedly subjected to unwanted advances from talent agents early in his career.
During a recent episode of "The Engelbert Humperdinck Show," the 90-year-old British singer opened up about the struggles he faced while pursuing a music career in his early 20s.

Humperdinck recalled that he began traveling from his hometown of Leicester, England, to London in the late 1950s in hopes of establishing himself as a singer. He said that at the time, his older sister was able to give him just enough money to spend one night in a hotel while he visited talent agents.

story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Urker died at his Louisiana home on his birthday Thursday, Oct. 1, Fox News Digital confirmed. He was 34.
