title: Matthew McConaughey says Woody Harrelson’s wild antics include 2 am visits, inviting strangers on vacations
summary: Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson share outrageous stories from their decades-long friendship, including a possible DNA test revelation.
story: McConaughey said his "hands couldn't keep up with my mouth" as he tried to sing and play music at the same time in his new film, "The Rivals of Amziah King."
Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson's friendship has put both of them in some wild situations.
While promoting their new show, "Brothers," the two actors, and close friends, have shared many anecdotes from their years-long friendship, which have sent the internet buzzing.

Whether it be finding out they might be brothers to Harrelson surprising McConaughey in bed in the middle of the night, these two Hollywood icons have made it clear they have an interesting friendship.
Harrelson and McConaughey have shared many crazy stories from their years-long friendship. (Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV via Getty Images)
Here are some of the most outrageous stories the two shared during recent interviews.
MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY'S PIECE OF RELATIONSHIP ADVICE THAT KEEPS HIS MARRIAGE TO CAMILA ALVES STRONG
Late-night surprise
McConaughey shared Harrelson once climbed into his bed at 2 in the morning. (Shea Kastriner/USTA via Getty Images)
During an appearance on the "Glass Half Full" podcast, McConaughey described some of the oddities that come with being Harrelson's friend, saying "he's never gone through a front door in his life."
He explained that no matter how long it has been since they last saw each other, Harrelson has "never called or sent a message" to make plans, adding, "he just shows up."

"We hadn't seen each other for a year at the time when I was living out in LA. I hadn't seen him for a year. Guess my introduction to him," he said. "My wife goes 'ah.' And I go, 'Woah.' Two in the morning, wake up, Woody's in between us in bed! He had jumped the fence, picked the window, snuck in, and got in bed with us."
When host Craig Melvin told Harrelson that "people have been shot for less," the actor replied, "Well, I was hoping he didn't have a gun."
"But what a good way to wake up a friend, you know what I mean, and get to be next to Camila [Alves, McConaughey's wife]," Harrelson added. "Like, that was nice. She was warm to me."
Anniversary confusion
Harrelson and McConaughey have different accounts of when they first met. (David M. Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images)
When speaking to Melvin, the celebrity duo also shared how they first met, although they admit they have different recollections.
McConaughey admits Harrelson "believes we've known each other one year longer" than he does, because "I don't remember the first time we met."
He blames it on the idea that they began taking shots together at 1 p.m., but when Harrelson corrected him on a detail in the story, McConaughey told him, "I don't remember. You tell me."

"I already knew of him and I liked him from a distance," Harrelson said. "And then I met him, and I'm like, 'Hey, let's do a shot,' and he's like, 'Man, I got a lot of work to do today.' I said, 'One shot's gonna stop you from all the work you got?'"
McConaughey then chimed in adding, "Hence, I don't remember meeting that day. It doesn't sound like that was the beginning and the end of the story."
Living on the edge
McConaughey once witnessed Harrelson do a handstand on the edge of a canyon. (Gary Miller/FilmMagic)
While telling Melvin about Harrelson's many talents, McConaughey casually mentioned that the actor once "did a handstand 18 inches away from the edge of the Grand Canyon."

"The stuff this guy pulls off because he didn't know better is still amazing," McConaughey said. "Most people do that stuff when they're a kid, and they lose it as they get older, because you know better. This kid, what are you, 60 what now... 65 and he's still doing handstands on the edge of the Grand Canyon."
While Harrelson tried to downplay the achievement by saying he was farther away than McConaughey is saying and that it wasn't the Grand Canyon, the "Dallas Buyers Club" star continued to praise him.
"I'm probably exaggerating less than from the edge on his hand, the Grand Canyon," McConaughey said. "The photographer freaks out. Never got a picture of it."
He added that had the photographer been able to take a photo, "it would have been the most epic shot."
Vacation antics
Harrelson once invited strangers to join him and McConaughey on vacation. (Chloe Kern/FilmMagic)
While promoting the new show, the two actors also sat down with Conan O'Brien on his podcast, "Conan O'Brien Needs A Friend."

During the interview, McConaughey shared an unbelievable story about the time Harrelson met a couple on their honeymoon while waiting for his luggage at baggage claim in Greece, and invited them to stay with him and McConaughey in the house McConaughey had rented for them and their families.

"You have a consistent habit of having an open heart and inviting people into your future life or yours or mine," McConaughey told Harrelson during the interview. "He's doing this routinely. He's, he's very consistent. We go on a Greek holiday and my family… we rent the place... We rent the place and they… we fly over, but they get there before us and we show up and there's two people sitting on the tailgate of a truck right in front of our rental."

He went on to say that at first he thought it was Harrelson and his wife Laura, but soon found out it was two strangers who told him, "We met Woody and Laura at the airport getting our luggage and… they're great."
When he confronted Harrelson, who had already claimed the primary bedroom in the rental, he told him, "They're great, man. They're going to be with us for a week."
Break-in
McConaughey shared that Harrelson would often break into his home and sometimes stay for months at a time. (Todd Williamson/NBC via Getty Images)
When speaking with People, McConaughey expanded on the idea that Harrelson would show up at his home "unannounced," calling it "one of Woody's great traits."

"He never comes through a front door. And he’ll swing by for an hour to say, ‘Howdy!’" McConaughey said. "It might turn into, ‘I’ve moved in for three months.’ It’s a beautiful trait how he makes himself at home."

Harrelson confirmed he does make a habit of making McConaughey's house his own, noting, McConaughey "tolerates it."
McConaughey went on to explain that often during these months-long stays, he will approach Harrelson after a while asking him to leave, and his kids will fight back.

"There are times when I’m like, ‘Man, Woody, I need some space,’ and my whole family’s like, ‘No, don’t let Woody go. We’ve been staying up later having more milkshakes,’ whatever," McConaughey said. "The laughter’s been in the house a while."
Brothers?
Harrelson and McConaughey found out there was a chance they may be brothers. (Apple TV press site)

In their new show, McConaughey and Harrelson play fictionalized versions of themselves who find out they could potentially be brothers.

The premise for the show seems outrageous. However, it is closer to the truth than it may seem, as the two actors found out during a trip to Greece with their families that there is a possibility the two may actually be brothers.

"In Greece a few years ago, we’re sitting around talking about how close we are and our families and et cetera and my mom is there. And she says, ‘Woody, I knew your dad,’" McConaughey told Kelly Ripa on her podcast in 2023.
McConaughey explained to Ripa that his mother and father were divorced before he was born, so there is a possibility that she and Harrelson's father met during that time period.
Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey star in "Brothers." (Apple TV press site)

Harrelson also told the story while on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" in 2023 that McConaughey's mom's story was "filled with innuendo," implying she and his father may have had a romance when they knew each other.
"The year of his birth, nine months before, she was on a sabbatical from her relationship with his supposed father, Jim," Harrelson joked about McConaughey’s birthday.

title: Robert Blake’s son returns to restaurant tied to family tragedy for new murder mystery
summary: Noah Blake opens "A Killer Night in Studio City" at Vitello's, confronting decades of pain tied to his father Robert Blake's infamous trial.
story: Actor Noah Blake returns to Vitello’s with a new murder mystery show. The "Teen Witch" alum says it marks a personal step toward healing and forging an identity beyond his family’s past.

Twenty-five years after Vitello's became part of a painful chapter in his family's history, Noah Blake has returned to the restaurant to direct and star in a fictional murder mystery, describing the production as part of his healing journey.
The "Teen Witch" alum's "A Killer Night in Studio City," a noir-inspired immersive theater production set in 1958, opened at the famed Italian restaurant on Sept. 15.

"When I was first approached about this, of course, there was this little bit of ... and then I was like, 'Wait, what am I doing? Of course, I should do this,'" Blake told Fox News Digital. "This is a chance for me to, not rewrite history, but to create a new page and to create a new connection and a new relationship for me with this place, for my name with this place, for my family with this place."
ROBERT BLAKE DEAD AT 89

Noah Blake (right) stars in "A Killer Night in Studio City," which is described as "an immersive murder mystery where classic Hollywood glamour collides with scandal, ambition, romance, and murder." (Wes Chappell)

"I've got a four-year-old son," Blake said. "I want him to be able to go there and enjoy Vitello's as he's grown up, God willing, as long as Vitello's is there. And I don't want him to ever feel funny. I want him to think about, 'Oh, Vitello's, that's the place where daddy did that fun show.' Not this other stuff. I'm not trying to minimize that tragedy, but it wasn't my tragedy, and it was a cross that I've had to bear and still will probably for the rest of my life."
"A Killer Night in Studio City" is held inside The Velvet Martini Lounge inside Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

Blake said Vitello's was a regular gathering place for his family while he was growing up, but he stayed away for decades. He eventually returned and agreed to stage the production there, saying he wanted to reclaim positive memories of a place he had loved.
Vitello's Restaurant in Los Angeles is seen here on May 5, 2001. (Getty Images)

"I want to go and do something in this space that is creative, that is fun, that is exciting, where people come and laugh and gasp and have a great time," he explained. "Some people may not even know [what happened] and the people who do might be curious and go, 'Oh, that has nothing to do with anything, and I had a great time.'"
WATCH: NOAH BLAKE SAYS RETURN TO SITE TIED TO FAMILY TRAGEDY IS ‘FULL CIRCLE’
The history Blake is trying to move beyond dates back to 2001, when his father Robert Blake's wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed after the couple had dinner at Vitello's.

The actor was acquitted of murder in 2005 in connection with Bakley's killing. Bakley was shot and killed while sitting in Robert's car near the restaurant. A civil jury later found him liable for her death and ordered him to pay Bakley's family $30 million, prompting him to file for bankruptcy, according to The Associated Press.
Robert Blake in a scene from the 1967 movie "In Cold Blood." (Dukas/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
An appeals court later reduced the award to $15 million, after which the parties reached a confidential settlement. Robert died in 2023 at 89.

Robert Blake, star of the 1970s show "Baretta," stands in court with his attorney M. Gerald Schwartzback on Sept. 17, 2004, for a pretrial conference. Blake was accused of murdering his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, who was found shot dead in her car in Los Angeles in May 2001. (Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)
Rose Lenore, Bakley's daughter with Robert, feels differently about the production. She told Fox News Digital that Vitello's remains too painful for her and others who loved her mother.

"I think him doing it at Vitello's is upsetting for me and anyone who loved Bonny," she said. "And there were quite a few people who did. She left behind three children, plus me. She also left behind a sister, my aunt, who misses her dearly. And so, to have Robert Blake's son do any show at Vitello's, let alone a murder mystery show, I find that to be insensitive and upsetting."
Bonny Lee Bakley, 44, was murdered on May 4, 2001. (ZUMA Press/ZUMA Archive / Shutterstock)

"I don't even care what the show is about," Lenore said. "I'm also not here to invalidate anyone's healing journey, if that's what this is for him. But I also think it's my moral obligation to stand up for what I believe in. I would still be upset if he was doing anything else. And for Noah to be doing a happy, fun show — I think it's in poor taste."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Rose Lenore Blake attends the Los Angeles screening of "Happy Anniversary" at LOOK Dine-In Cinemas Glendale in Glendale, California, on Jan. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

"I'm not wishing any harm on Noah," Lenore continued. "I wish him well in his life and career. But it would be hard for me to stay silent on something like this. It would be hard for me to stay silent about my mother."

Responding to Lenore's criticism, Blake wrote in a statement to Fox News Digital, "I have my own deeply personal reasons for doing this play. Vitello's was a place that I loved my entire life. Over time, that place became the physical embodiment for me of a much larger and devastating chapter of my life — one thing that I had nothing to do with, but whose consequences I have had to endure for years."
Noah Blake is seen here with his father Robert Blake during happier times. (Courtesy of Noah Blake)

"Choosing to walk back into that space now and create something uniquely mine — something lighthearted and entertaining that people are enjoying — is part of my own healing journey," he wrote. "It's about taking a place that had come to represent something painfully dark in my life and allowing it to represent something else. I'm not erasing history or rewriting it. I'm simply adding a new page to it, and I don't ask or expect anyone else to sign off on what I need to do to heal."

Actor Robert Blake and his son Noah Blake pause in front of the coffin bearing Bonny Lee Bakley on May 25, 2001, during a funeral ceremony in Los Angeles. Behind them are Robert Blake's assistant, Earle Caldwell, and an unidentified woman. (Getty Images)

"Rose is absolutely entitled to her feelings," Blake continued. "I've been there for her many times over the years, and I care for her. She chose to express her feelings about this publicly, which certainly wouldn't have been my choice and still isn't. I would much rather have had a private conversation with her. I've reached out and asked her to call me so that we could talk about this, and that conversation has yet to happen. But that door remains open for her."
Blake said returning to Vitello's has also forced him to revisit his complicated relationship with his late father.

Noah Blake (left) told Fox News Digital he hopes to one day make a documentary exploring his father Robert Blake's case, sitting down with those who knew the actor in an effort to better understand what happened the night his wife, Bonny Lee Bakley, was killed. (WireImage)

"I don't think people really realize when something like that happens, how many lives are impacted in such a profound way," he explained. "I had to wrestle with who my father really was for everything I thought he was or knew or saw him as. Did he do this thing? Was he really capable of this? Was he that far gone? Was my father this monster?"

Actor Robert Blake speaks exclusively to Barbara Walters from the Los Angeles County Jail, where he is being held without bail on charges of killing his wife, Bonnie Lee Bakley. Blake said he did the interview for his then-3-year-old daughter, Rosie. His first and only televised interview from jail aired on "20/20" on Wednesday, Feb. 26, 2003. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"It's tough because it makes you question a lot. 'What is my genetic makeup?' It was years of intense scrutiny, and it was impossible to live my life, and for other people as well. It's not cool to know that this guy's son had a nervous breakdown and couldn't leave his house for six months and was having panic attacks and night sweats and was incapable of functioning."
Robert Blake poses with his children Delinah and Noah at the Emmy Awards in Pasadena, California, in September 1977. (Getty Images)

"There were moments my father could be a very loving, kind, decent, generous human being," he said. "And there were times when he could just be an absolute f---ing monster and just the worst kind of selfish and menacing and threatening."

"A Killer Night in Studio City" is running through Halloween. (Wes Chappell)
Before his death, Robert fiercely denied murdering Bakley.

For Blake, returning to the restaurant carries a meaning beyond the fictional story he says he wants to tell. While he recognizes the connection others may make to his family's past, Blake stressed he does not want that history to define him.
Noah Blake told Fox News Digital he wants to create new memories at Vitello's. (Wes Chappell)

title: Phil Collins gets frank on marriage failures and life regrets: 'I regret my marriages falling apart'
summary: Phil Collins told Piers Morgan his Genesis touring schedule destroyed his first marriage and revealed deep regrets about all three marriages falling apart.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Phil Collins is opening up about his biggest regret throughout the course of his career.
During a recent interview on "Piers Morgan Uncensored," the 75-year-old musician reflected on the toll his career took on his relationships with his children and how it affected his three marriages.

"To some extent, I have to say I regret my marriages falling apart," he explained. "Sometimes I jumped. Well, one time I jumped, two times I was pushed. But I wouldn't have written it like that. But on the other hand, I've got five fantastic kids that I wouldn't have if that hadn't happened. So I have to balance it."
The famous drummer was married to his first wife, Andrea Bertorelli, from 1975 to 1980. Collins adopted Bertorelli's daughter, Joely, and the couple welcomed son Simon.
PHIL COLLINS' BRUSH WITH DEATH LEFT HIS CHILDREN PREPARING FOR THE UNTHINKABLE
Collins shared his biggest regret over the course of his career. (Gina Wetzler/Redferns)

He also shares daughter Lily with his second wife, Jill Tavelman, whom he was married to from 1984 to 1996, and sons Nicholas and Mathew with his third wife, Orianne Cevey, whom he was married to from 1999 to 2006.
When looking back on his first marriage, Collins admitted it broke down because he wasn't around, as he was touring with his band, Genesis, and couldn't be home.

"Genesis did, in one year, I think, three American tours, two European tours, and a tour of Japan. And when I ended up getting separated from my first wife, the guys in the band said, ‘Well, why didn’t you tell us? We’d have stopped it.’ But that’s easy to say in retrospect," he said. "I was gone, and we grew apart."

Despite his failure to make his relationships with his wives work, Collins said he "always tried to be there for the kids," and that he never planned on getting married three times, noting, "You don't go into life thinking that."

"I'm learning how to accept your actions and vocalize how they made me feel," she wrote in an excerpt read by Morgan. "I accept and honor the sadness and anger I felt toward the things you did or didn't do, did or didn't give me. I forgive you for not always being there when I needed it, for not being the dad I expected. I forgive the mistakes you made. And although it may seem like it's too late, it's not. title: 'Caddyshack' star Michael O'Keefe claims cocaine was budgeted on set, admits filming scenes high
summary: Michael O'Keefe opens up about rampant cocaine use on the "Caddyshack" set, saying people treated the drug "like it was toothpaste" in the '70s.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Michael O'Keefe is getting candid about what it was like on the set of the hit 1980 movie "Caddyshack."

During a recent interview with Page Six, the 71-year-old actor shared that there was a lot of cocaine on the set of the classic comedy and claimed the drug was even accounted for in the movie's budget, with the actor noting, "there was some miscellaneous item."
"It was the 70s," he said. "That’s what was happening back then. People were just treating it like it was toothpaste, and you had to do it twice a day to stay healthy."
The movie was filmed in 1979 and released in 1980, and also starred Ted Knight, Chevy Chase, Bill Murray and Rodney Dangerfield and was set at the fictional Bushwood Country Club.
O'Keefe recalled doing cocaine before filming certain scenes in "Caddyshack." (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)
TOM HARDY'S 'MOBLAND' DRAMA TOPS HOLLYWOOD'S MOST NOTORIOUS ON-SET MELTDOWNS AND FEUDS

When reflecting on the drug use on set, O'Keefe recalled doing cocaine before filming certain scenes, telling Page Six that when he watches those scenes now, "it was not my favorite memory," and that he is "not too happy about them."

"But I can report to you that right after that movie, during that movie, was the last time I ever did anything like cocaine," he said. "I realized that it was a terrible thing to get involved [with], and like so many things in the drug world, it looked like fun, but in reality, it wasn’t."
Part of the reason he decided to take a step back from drugs was the death of Doug Kenney, who co-wrote and produced "Caddyshack."
He called Kenney's death "a huge wake-up call." Kenney died at 33 after falling from a cliff in Hawaii in 1980.

"[He was] one of the most affable, intelligent, funny people in the world. … Was strung out on cocaine, got depressed, and committed suicide," he said. "It was truly a result of drug addiction, and that was a huge wake-up call."
Prior to starring in "Caddyshack," O'Keefe had his breakthrough starring in "The Great Santini," which earned him an Academy Award nomination for best supporting actor.

He later starred in "Ironweed," "Frozen River" and, most recently, the Apple TV series "Your Friends & Neighbors," in which he plays Ron Cooper, the father of Jon Hamm's Andrew "Coop" Cooper. His most recognizable role remains Danny Noonan in "Caddyshack."

title: Chris Rock shreds 'woke 1.0' era, compares modern outrage to Salem witch hunts
summary: Chris Rock compares cancel culture to Salem witch hunts and the Old Testament, arguing wokeness also needs to come with a willingness to forgive.
story: Former Superman star says the industry is emerging from its 'woke era,' explains why filmmakers are fleeing California, and reveals what comes next
Chris Rock is getting candid about the importance of forgiveness in a world so quick to cancel others.

During a recent appearance on "The Daily" podcast, the 61-year-old comedian discussed his issues with "wokeness," saying that while advocating for marginalized people and giving them a voice is great, it needs to come with forgiveness.

"The problem with wokeness is we're in the Old Testament right now," he said. "And the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn't work. So they had to write a remix called the New Testament."

Host David Marchese then asked if he thought there was "anything redeeming" that came out of the post-George Floyd era, which he referred to as "woke 1.0," since Democratic politicians now seem to be straying further from that ideology now.
Rock compared wokeness to the Salem witch trials. (Jemal Countess/WireImage)
SKILLET'S JOHN COOPER SAYS WOKE ACTIVISTS HAVE 'BIG HEARTS' BUT ARE 'HURTING THEMSELVES'
The "Grown Ups" star reiterated his position that "it's great to help those that need help," but noted the problem comes "when you institutionalize it."

"The Salem witch hunts. I'm sure the first three witches they caught were actually f- - -ing witches," he said. "But then you open up a witch office and now you've got to start lying. Now you've gotta f- - - ing make s- - - up because you've got overhead. You've got to justify the witch hunters f - - -ing pensions and s- - -."

He explained that just because he advocates for forgiveness, it "doesn't mean condoning abusive behavior. You can reprimand your friends," adding that holding them accountable is "also part of friendship."
"If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends," he said.
Rock said part of friendship is holding each other accountable. (Leon Bennett/EveryStory2026/WireImage)

While he admits there is room for improvement when it comes to cancel culture and wokeness, he noted he is "glad that all of this stuff happened," as it allowed for certain voices to be heard which otherwise may not have been.
Kaivan Shroff — a former Hillary Clinton campaign staffer – disagreed with Rock, telling Fox News Digital the comedian "is oversimplifying this in a way that is pretty self-serving."

"Sometimes the problem is not that people ‘took a joke out of context.’ Often the context is perfectly clear and the comedian knows exactly who the joke is aimed at, knows a lot of people will find it offensive, and is counting on that discomfort to make the material feel edgy or viral," Shroff said. "You don’t get to use outrage as part of the act and then act shocked when the outrage follows."
Rock is currently promoting his new film, "Misty Green," which he wrote and directed in addition to starring in it.
Rock is currently promoting his new film, "Misty Green." (Rosalind O'Connor/NBC via Getty Images)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

The film follows an award-winning actress, Misty Green, who is working hard to make a comeback after years of watching her career slowly fade away, with Rock portraying a casting director who once worked with the actress.

"I'm really into expiration dates. I have a lot of friends who are in their 50s or whatever and there's this thing everybody tells you, ‘You can do art forever.’ And that's just not true," he said. "And a lot of show business has, like you've got to reach certain plateaus by a certain time or else you're going to be in trouble. So yeah, Misty is turning 40 and there's a little bit of an expiration date happening here. I wanted to do a movie about Hollywood. I wanted to do a movie about the expiration dates we all have."

He said he also wanted to make a movie about Los Angeles, calling it a "tale of two cities," noting that while there is "sunshine and palm trees," people are also "constantly walking over homeless people."

The actor previously spoke about the message he wanted to get across when making the film, telling Variety in September that much of the movie is about Los Angeles, which he called a "complicated place" that "attracts an underbelly that people want to pretend doesn’t exist."

story: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path during an interview at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards March 26, 2026, in Los Angeles.

title: Michael Douglas confirms secret affair with Kathleen Turner on 'Romancing the Stone' set
summary: Michael Douglas reveals in his memoir, "One Helluva Ride," that he and Kathleen Turner kept their "Romancing the Stone" affair secret for 40 years.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Michael Douglas is confirming a rumor that has followed him around for decades.

In an excerpt from his upcoming memoir, "One Helluva Ride," the 82-year-old actor revealed he and Kathleen Turner had an affair while filming "Romancing the Stone," a rumor they denied for over 40 years.

"Kathleen was smart, funny, and sexy with a deep, sultry voice that became her signature," he wrote in an excerpt obtained by People. "I instantly liked her, and we were immediately attracted to each other."
He said, although he was married to Diandra Luker at the time, "things at home were in a bad place" and both he and Luker "were both having extramarital affairs."
MICHAEL DOUGLAS' ACADEMY AWARD-WINNING ROLE IN ‘WALL STREET’ WAS FIRST OFFERED TO THESE TWO A-LIST ACTORS
Douglas admitted he and Turner had an affair while filming "Romancing the Stone." (20th Century Fox/Getty Images)

Douglas wrote that he left home to film the 1984 movie "still technically married, but separated," and that while audiences were "certain for years that we were in a relationship together" while making the movie, they denied it, even through the making of the sequel and years later when they reunited on "The Kominsky Method."
The two told the public that while they "had amazing chemistry" and were "both tempted," they never acted on their feelings.

"The truth is that during the production of Romancing the Stone, Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship," he wrote. "It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen."
He noted that the two of them kept their affair a secret for 40 years to protect Luker and their son, Cameron.

"There were no cameras in elevators, no assistants using cell phones to take pictures," he said. "As Jack and Joan were falling in love, Kathleen and I were keeping the chemistry alive."
Douglas and Turner were falling in love as their characters were doing the same on screen. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

title: Prince William, Kate Middleton’s secret nicknames exposed as former staffer reveals palace WhatsApp habits
summary: Royal family WhatsApp nicknames exposed by a former staffer, from Prince William's "Bobcat" to Prince Harry's "Baz" and other secret aliases.
story: Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner shares the private nicknames reportedly used by Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles and other royals.
Behind palace doors, it's apparently less "Your Royal Highness" and more "Bobcat."

A former royal staffer is pulling back the curtain on Prince William and Kate Middleton's reported WhatsApp nicknames. Jack Stooks, who worked for King Charles for 21 years as a gardener at Highgrove, shared a rare glimpse into how members of the royal family reportedly identified one another on the messaging app.
"I remember Princes William and Harry always had the latest phones," Stooks explained to GB News.
"They actually gave their numbers out to staff so we could contact them about logistical things. They also had our numbers, and they would just WhatsApp us if they needed anything.
PRINCE WILLIAM AND KATE MIDDLETON’S ‘GENUINE LOVE STORY' IS BUILT ON BEING A 'VERY NORMAL FAMILY': AUTHOR

Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, are given a tour by Jamie Jones Buchanan, CEO of the Leeds Rhinos during a visit to AMT Headingley Stadium, the home of the Leeds Rhinos rugby team, Sept. 29, 2026 in Leeds, England.  (James Glossop/WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"We couldn't have them saved under their real names, so they had nicknames instead," said Stooks. "William was 'Bobcat', Harry was ‘Baz,’ and when Catherine joined the family, she became ‘Mrs. Bobcat.’"
Stooks told Fox News Digital on behalf of OLBG that only a limited number of staff were given the royals' phone numbers, which had to be kept a closely guarded secret.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, at the DMMI Royal Charity Polo Cup 2026 in Windsor, England, July 10, 2026. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"We had the family under different names, so that if anyone's phone was taken, the number could be differentiated," he explained. "That way, no one knew which number was which. They all change their numbers regularly, so I don't have any of their phone numbers now."

"The nickname I gave to Harry on my phone was ‘Baz,’" Stooks shared. "He was always called ‘Baz’ by his friends, so I just took that. From memory, William was ‘Wombat,’ again because that is what his friends called him."
Prince William drives a tractor alongside Catherine, Princess of Wales, during cleanup activities at Ettrick Bay on the Isle of Bute, Scotland, Sept. 17, 2026. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, meets well-wishers during a visit to the Millennium Powerhouse, a multiservice youth hub in the Moss Side neighborhood of Manchester, England, Nov. 16, 2023. (Getty Images)

"He may have a lot of privilege, but William was never one to demand something from staff," Stooks told the outlet. "He was really polite. He would always check how busy I was before asking me to do errands for him. And whenever I said I would do something for William, he would always reply, 'You're a legend.'

"They have groups with their friends, and there is also a family group with the royal cousins, including Prince William, Zara Tindall, Peter Phillips and the York sisters," he continued. "They're very much like any other family when it comes to keeping in touch through their phones."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, arrive for a visit to Southport Community Centre in Southport, England, Oct. 10, 2024. (Getty Images)

Several royal experts told Fox News Digital that members of the royal family have long used nicknames. Some are terms of affection, while others have reportedly been used as aliases for privacy or security.

(Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
"When they had a security issue, William and Kate are known as Danny Collins and Daphne Clark, DC," royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital.

"In other words, Duke and Duchess of Cambridge," he said, referring to the Prince and Princess of Wales. "The late queen was always known as Sharon, believe it or not, just for the simple S, which stood for sovereign.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, smiles as he rides in a boat during a tour of the Guapimirim mangrove area in Guanabara Bay, managed by the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, on Nov. 4, 2025, in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. (Aaron Chown-Pool/Getty Images)

When he started a romance with Queen Camilla, the joke started as well. That's where Fred and Gladys first started.

"And then you would think, ‘Why on earth would the queen, Elizabeth that is, be called any other nickname other than Your Majesty?’" he said. "Prince Philip used to call the queen Cabbage."
British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital the name derived from the French "mon petit chou," or "my little cabbage."
Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh, revisit Broadlands in Hampshire to mark their Diamond Wedding Anniversary on Nov. 20, 2007. (Tim Graham/Getty Images)
"I believe he also affectionately called her sausage," Chard added.

One of the royal family's best-known nicknames is "Lilibet." Then-Princess Elizabeth struggled to pronounce her own name as a toddler, and her grandfather, King George V, reportedly imitated her pronunciation. Her husband, Prince Philip, also affectionately called her "Lilibet," and the name was later chosen by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle for their daughter, Princess Lilibet.

"Courtiers have long referred to Prince Harry and the former Prince Andrew, as the 'Dukes of Hazard,' which needs no explanation," said Fordwich.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor and his ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, attend the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent, at Westminster Cathedral on Sept. 16, 2025, in London, England. (Mark Cuthbert/UK Press via Getty Images)

"When Kate is getting a little bit upset with William in any way, she starts using the names of 'Baldy' and ‘Big Willy,'" Turner alleged, a claim previously made by author Tom Quinn. A Kensington Palace spokesperson previously told Fox News Digital that the palace doesn't comment on books.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Michael McDonald’s long-lost son reveals stunning moment he discovered famous father after 58 years
summary: A St. Louis man adopted through Catholic Charities nearly 60 years ago learned his biological father is Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald.
story: Michael Goessling tells Fox News Digital how a mysterious call with a musician named ‘Mike’ led to an unbelievable realization with a quick internet search.

EXCLUSIVE: Michael Goessling always knew he was adopted. But what he did not know for nearly 58 years was that his biological father had one of the most recognizable and beloved voices in American music.

The St. Louis man learned recently that his father is five-time Grammy winner and Doobie Brothers singer Michael McDonald, a musician Goessling had admired since childhood and had unknowingly paid to see perform twice as a young man.

But even after receiving the letter that began it all, meeting his biological mother and learning his biological father was a mysterious musician named "Mike," Goessling still had no idea who was waiting on the other end of the phone.
RITA WILSON LEARNED ABOUT FATHER’S TRAGIC PAST, SECRET FAMILY IN BULGARIA ON TV SHOW
Michael Goessling, right, spoke with Fox News Digital about discovering at age 58 that Michael McDonald was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
The answer finally came during their first conversation, when "Mike" mentioned he was touring and would be stopping in St. Louis on Sept. 4 at a venue he believed was called "Hollywood."

Goessling thought of the Hollywood Casino Amphitheater and, puzzled that his biological father was apparently still a touring musician at his age, began searching the venue's concert schedule as the two men spoke.
The Doobie Brothers were playing in concert Sept. 4.
Suddenly, the pieces began falling into place: "Mike." Musician. That unmistakable voice.
"Are you Michael McDonald?" Goessling finally asked.
McDonald chuckled. "Yep, afraid so."
"Oh my gosh, this is getting crazier by the second," Goessling recalled saying. "I can't even, I can't get my head around this. This is too much."
"I know," McDonald replied. "Take a minute."
"I thought I was being punked for a second," Goessling told Fox News Digital. "It's like, 'No, this can't be real. This is impossible. What is going on here?'"
More than a year later, he said the discovery can still feel unreal.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS
Michael Goessling credits his adoptive parents, Paul and Kay Goessling, with giving him a "charmed" childhood. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
"I still wake up sometimes and my first thought is, ‘Oh my gosh, that was a crazy dream,’ only to realize that here we are."

The extraordinary phone call came just days after a letter ended a mystery stretching back to Goessling's birth. On May 6, 2025, an attorney representing his biological mother contacted Goessling to explain that she believed he was the son she had placed for adoption through Catholic Charities nearly 58 years earlier.
Goessling had always known he was adopted, but the adoption was closed. He knew nothing about his biological parents, and they knew virtually nothing about the life he had gone on to live.

His biological mother, he learned, had spent roughly 30 to 35 years searching for him. Both biological parents hoped he might be willing to communicate, Goessling recalled, but above all, they wanted to know that he was well.
"It was a wonderful surprise but quite a shock," he said. "It felt like a tsunami hit me."
Goessling called his biological mother that evening. Although he had never actively searched for his biological parents, he had long hoped he might someday have the opportunity to thank them.

"I just want you to hear from me that I got nothing but love for you," he recalled telling her. "This is such an amazing gift, that I get to thank you personally. … They were always heroes in my story," he said.
CUT OFF BY YOUR ADULT CHILD? PSYCHOLOGY RESEARCHER REVEALS WHAT PARENTS SHOULD DO NEXT
Michael Goessling said people compared his appearance to Michael McDonald years before he discovered the singer was his biological father. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Their first conversation lasted about 90 minutes. Goessling eventually proposed meeting for lunch that Friday, prompting his biological mother to remind him that Friday was his birthday.
"Yeah, yeah. You've waited long enough. I think I've waited enough," he recalled replying. "Let's meet on my birthday, 58 years to the day."

After a three-hour lunch and nearly six decades apart, Goessling learned there was someone else anxious to speak with him. His biological father had deliberately remained in the background so mother and son could have their reunion first.

"He really wanted the mother-son thing to happen first, which is just true to his character," Goessling said. "He thought that was very important, and he wanted to take a back seat so that could happen."
Before father and son connected, McDonald left Goessling a voicemail. That unmistakable voice immediately struck him.
"Whoa, what a voice," Goessling recalled telling his biological mother.
"Yeah, he gets that a lot," she replied with a chuckle.
The voice seemed strangely familiar, but Goessling still didn't make the connection. When the two men finally spoke, he began by telling McDonald what he had already told his biological mother.
"Thank you for giving me a shot in this world," Goessling recalled saying. "I've had a charmed life. And it all started with you guys."
Then he asked what his biological father did for a living.
"I'm a musician," McDonald told him.

Goessling, a lifelong music obsessive who once worked in the music business, thought that was terrific. It wasn't until the conversation turned to McDonald's upcoming tour stop that he finally put it together.
The revelation contained another coincidence almost too remarkable to invent; Goessling was already a huge fan.

The Doobie Brothers had been among his favorite bands since childhood, alongside The Who and Journey. He vividly remembers first hearing "Takin' It to the Streets" after McDonald joined the group and insisting to the person playing it that there had been some mistake.
"I know the Doobie Brothers and that is not the Doobie Brothers," Goessling remembered declaring as a child.
He soon learned about the band's new singer and became a McDonald fan, too. He remained one.

In fact, Goessling had already watched his biological father perform in concert twice, once in the 1980s, and again in the early 1990s, without ever imagining that the man onstage was the father whose identity he did not know.
When Fox News Digital pointed out that meant he had actually paid twice to see his own father perform, Goessling laughed.
"I should get reimbursed for that."

There were other clues hiding in plain sight. After Goessling grew out his hair and white beard during the COVID-19 pandemic, people began telling him they liked the "Michael McDonald thing" he had going on.
"Little did I know, five years later that that would resonate even so true," he said.

After the families met, the similarities became even harder to miss. During a visit with McDonald, Goessling said McDonald's wife, Amy, and his newfound half-sister would watch him do or say something and suddenly burst out laughing.
Michael McDonald of The Doobie Brothers in 2021. McDonald has a new memoir titled, "What a Fool Believes."  (Chris Pizzello/AP Photo, File)

"Your dad does the exact same thing," they would tell him. "They couldn't take their eyes off me," Goessling said. "They're waiting to see what I would do or say next because there was so many just natural similarities."
Yet, for Goessling, the remarkable celebrity connection is not the part of his story that matters most.

Learning where he came from also meant finally understanding what his biological parents had faced nearly six decades earlier, when they were just two 14-year-old eighth-graders confronting a pregnancy that would change all three of their lives.

According to Goessling, the teenagers' initial reaction was that they would marry, raise their baby and rely on their families to help them. Their parents concluded they were simply too young at the time.
"They were just far too young to be married and to have a child," Goessling said.
Their families ultimately determined that adoption would be best, he said, although relinquishing their son had not been his biological parents' first choice.
Nearly six decades later, Goessling sees what happened through the lens of both gratitude and faith.
"Mike, I mean, he wasn't Michael McDonald [then]. He was Mike from the neighborhood," he said, imagining how differently life could have been had two 14-year-olds attempted to raise a child together.
Patrick Simmons, left, Tom Johnston, John McFee, Marc Russo, Michael McDonald and Ed Toth of The Doobie Brothers perform onstage in Pacific Palisades, Calif. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for BC, File)

"I have to believe that it all worked out as it was supposed to because, certainly, when I see us all now together, it's just the greatest joy," Goessling said. "I think this was the plan. And I think it was a beautiful plan."

That plan, as Goessling sees it, led him to Paul and Kay Goessling. He grew up in a family of four children. Three were adopted before, against the odds, Kay became pregnant with their youngest daughter, Linda.
Goessling describes his childhood as "charmed" and said he could not have chosen better parents himself.
"If I could go back and pick two folks, I would pick them and do it all over again," he said. "They were just the most wonderful blessing in my life."
His father, Paul, died shortly before Christmas 2024 after a long battle with Parkinson's disease, and Goessling said the two were extremely close. Six months later, another father entered his life.
"After losing my father, I get a letter, and Mike pops up," Goessling said. "Another father enters my life, my world."
Kay's reaction to the discovery was immediate. When Goessling showed her the letter, he said his mother began crying and declared what had happened "a miracle."
Michael Goessling with his adoptive father, Paul Goessling. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Michael Goessling, here with his siblings many decades ago, credits his adoptive parents with giving him a "charmed" childhood. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
She asked whether he had met his biological mother, and he had.
"Oh my God, go get her," Goessling recalled Kay saying. "I have to meet her. I've got a million questions. What's she like? I gotta give her a big hug."
Goessling said his mother has embraced his biological family from the beginning, and the once-separate branches of his family came together with surprising ease.
"Everybody's in love with everybody," he said.
Father and son now speak frequently and text "all the time," according to Goessling.
And while the identity of his biological father is what thrust his story into the spotlight, Goessling hopes the attention gives him an opportunity to talk about adoption as a blessing.

A practicing Catholic who was raised in the faith and adopted through Catholic Charities, Goessling said his parents taught him from childhood to understand his adoption not as evidence that he had been unwanted, but as evidence that he was deeply loved.
Michael McDonald and Michael Goessling with family. (Courtesy of Michael Goessling)
Even before he was old enough to fully understand what adoption meant, he knew how his parents viewed it.
"It was a miracle," he said. "It was the greatest thing. It was a gift from God."
Only when Goessling grew old enough to understand where babies came from, he said, did he fully appreciate the significance of the decisions that had been made before his birth.

"Obviously, we all know there are choices in this world, and I am so grateful and fortunate for the choices they made on my behalf," he said. "Adoption has been absolutely nothing but a blessing for me. … I celebrate adoption and I always have. It's always been a big part of my life story."
Now, nearly six decades later, Goessling has been able to thank the biological parents he once could only imagine, and discovered that they had spent those same decades wondering about him.
He hopes the unlikely circumstances that brought attention to his family can help "elevate" the conversation surrounding adoption.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I want this to elevate the narrative, the adoption narrative," he said. "I want that adoption gets celebrated more in this country. If my crazy story can be true, Lord knows anything is possible."
And if Michael McDonald is watching? Goessling doesn't need an interview to deliver the message. He said father and son already talk regularly.
"I just tell him that I love him, and I tell him thank you for everything," he said.
After 58 years, the man who says he never felt deprived of a family has somehow ended up with an even larger one.
"My cup overflows," Goessling said.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: 'Piano Man' Billy Joel's prized motorcycle collection hits the auction block
summary: Billy Joel's prized motorcycle collection of over 70 lots hits the auction block at Retromobile New York, featuring Ducati, Triumph and more.
story: Gooding Christie's founder David Gooding told Fox News Digital that Billy Joel is a "genuine enthusiast" who loves all kinds of motorcycles.
Billy Joel may be right, or he may be crazy as his prized motorcycle collection hits the auction block in the Big Apple.
More than 70 lots from the Piano Man's personal collection will be offered without reserve during Gooding Christie's inaugural auction at Retromobile New York next month.

Joel, 77, "is a genuine enthusiast who loves all sorts of motorcycles," Gooding Christie's founder, David Gooding, exclusively told Fox News Digital of the array of two-wheelers going up for sale, which includes "older bikes, bikes with side cars ... a mixture of everything."
BILLY JOEL SAYS LOUD ROCK CONCERTS DAMAGED HIS NERVES, LED TO HIS BRAIN SURGERY AND NPH DIAGNOSIS
The "Piano Man" is an avid motorcycle enthusiast and will auction off over 70 items. (Billy Joel archives)
"The exciting thing is all the motorcycles are being sold without reserve," Gooding said, meaning the auction will be sold to the highest bidder regardless of the final price.
BILLY JOEL SAYS AGING MUSICIANS WHO KEEP MAKING RECORDS PAST THEIR PRIME 'DILUTE THEIR LEGACY'

"And, a portion of the proceeds are going to benefit the Joel Foundation, which is a wonderful charity. It's a great charity that supports non-profit music education, public women's health ... there's some great initiatives that it supports."
The collection includes a number of his most cherished motorcycles, including Ducati, BMW, Moto Guzzi, Harley-Davidson, Yamaha, Triumph, Honda, Kawasaki, and more.
Joel's 1975 Ducati 750 Sport is up for auction through the Gooding Christie's sale. (Mike Maez, Gooding & Company, LLC.)

"One of the stars of the sale is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville that was gifted to Billy Joel by Madison Square Garden to commemorate 150 sold out shows," Gooding said of the bike, which is expected to retrieve anywhere from $10,000 - $15,000.
"He still holds the record for the most sold out show of anyone ever at Madison Square Garden. And this bike is painted with a keyboard on the tank. It's really, really a special, special item."

The custom-painted motorcycle was commissioned especially for Joel, and is accompanied by a matching helmet listing every single show and year he played at Madison Square Garden, according to Gooding.

Among the most captivating motorcycles in the collection is a 1978 Triumph T140 Bonneville gifted to Mr. Joel by Madison Square Garden on the occasion of his 150th sold-out show at the world-famous venue. (Mike Maez, Gooding & Company, LLC.)

The collection also includes an iconic 1982 Ducati 900 Mike Hailwood Replica, which is estimated between $15,000-$25,000, marketed by Ducati to commemorate the motorcycle that Mike Hailwood rode to his legendary comeback victory at the 1978 Isle of Man.

A restored 1975 Ducati 750 Sport is estimated at $25,000 - $35,000 without reserve, and is "one of the most beautiful motorcycles ever conceived," according to the auction house.
Motorcycles from the auction – which is slated for Nov. 20-21 – will be on display at the Javits Center in New York.
Gooding Christie’s announced the world-famous Billy Joel Motorcycle Collection as a leading consignment for its upcoming inaugural sale at the Javits Center in New York City. (Billy Joel Archives)
Billy Joel has been collecting motorcycles for decades. (Larry Busacca/Getty Images)

"The great thing about this collection is it's certainly going to appeal to Billy Joel's fan base, but I also believe there are many people that are going to just be very passionate about motorcycles themselves," Gooding said.
"So we've got this sort of dual pool of interested buyers because the bikes in and of themselves are really important and valuable and exciting, and then you've got the Billy Joel component."

"I’ve always been drawn to bikes built by people who cared about getting every detail right," Joel said in a statement shared through Gooding Christie's. "I’ve loved building this collection. Now it’s someone else’s turn to hit the road."

The "Uptown Girl" singer underwent brain surgery after revealing his normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) diagnosis in May 2025. NPH affects his vision, hearing and balance, according to a statement Joel released on social media at the time.
Billy Joel announced his normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) diagnosis in May 2025. (Myrna M. Suarez/Getty Images)
During a recent appearance on his self-titled SiriusXM show, "The Billy Joel Channel," the legendary singer said doctors told him that his rock 'n' roll lifestyle caused damage to his brain nerves.

At the time of the announcement, Joel was forced to cancel a number of shows and said his condition had been "exacerbated by recent concert performances, leading to problems with hearing, vision and balance."

NPH is a condition that happens when cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside the skull and presses on the brain. This condition is most likely to occur in people over age 65. Treating this condition involves surgery to implant a shunt to drain excess fluid from the inside of the skull, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

title: Johnny Depp's return in 'Ebenezer' divides fans as new trailer sparks debate
summary: Johnny Depp's transformation as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer sparked debate over its "think again" tagline and revisionist marketing.
story: FOX Nation host Nancy Grace reacts to officials finding the remains of a missing Colorado mom and previews her exclusive interview with Jonny Depp’s attorney Camille Vasquez at CrimeCon 2023, streaming now on FOX Nation.
Johnny Depp is back in action – and his latest transformation quickly stirred up a spirited reaction.

The actor’s turn as Ebenezer Scrooge in the new "Ebenezer" trailer released Thursday earned enthusiastic praise from fans, while the film’s suggestion that audiences should "think again" about the classic story left others scratching their heads.

"From the trailer I can confirm, its still the same story," one X user wrote in response to the trailer. "It's the same as Scrooge, and Muppets Christmas Carol. So dw about having to think again, you really don't."

"Why is the tagline 'Think you know his story? Think again.' when every single thing in the trailers is faithful to Dickens?" another questioned. "That is his story and we all know it. This might be a good version, but why is it being marketed as revisionist? What story do you think we think we know?"
JOHNNY DEPP SAYS HE WAS A 'CRASH TEST DUMMY FOR METOO,' ACCUSES HOLLYWOOD PALS OF ABANDONING HIM TO 'GO WOKE'
Johnny Depp transformed into Scrooge for the upcoming film "Ebenezer." (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)
Despite some skepticism over the film’s marketing, other fans were eager to see Depp put his own spin on the oft-told Christmas tale.
"So many have done this story and I still will watch it."

The excitement over Depp’s return comes as "Ebenezer" marks his first major Hollywood studio film in years. The actor last appeared on the big screen in the 2023 French historical drama "Jeanne du Barry" and later stepped behind the camera to direct "Modi: Three Days on the Wing of Madness." He is also set to star opposite Penélope Cruz in the upcoming thriller "Day Drinker."

For some fans, Depp’s latest slate of projects signaled that the longtime Hollywood star was firmly back in action.

"Depp is back at the top of his game!" another added.

Johnny Depp is seen attending a screening of his show "21 Jump Street." (Barry King/WireImage)

Depp made his film debut in "A Nightmare on Elm Street" in 1984 before becoming a teen idol as undercover police officer Tom Hanson on the television series "21 Jump Street." His career took a major turn with Tim Burton’s "Edward Scissorhands" in 1990.

His portrayal of Jack Sparrow turned "Pirates of the Caribbean" into a blockbuster franchise and earned Depp his first Academy Award nomination. He received two more Oscar nominations for "Finding Neverland" and "Sweeney Todd," winning a Golden Globe for the latter.

Johnny Depp's career was affected by his highly publicized legal battle with ex-wife Amber Heard. (Getty Images)
But Depp’s decades of Hollywood success eventually gave way to a turbulent period in his career.
Depp's disappearance from the big screen came after a few box-office failures, his highly publicized legal battle with ex-wife Amber Heard along with personal troubles.

In 2020, Depp lost a U.K. libel case against The Sun over an article that called him a "wife beater." Two years later, he faced Heard in a high-profile Virginia defamation trial over her 2018 Washington Post op-ed about domestic abuse. A jury found Heard liable for defaming Depp.

title: Alzheimer’s risk linked to compound found in popular joint health supplements
summary: University of Florida researchers found glucosamine users with mild cognitive impairment were 25% more likely to progress to dementia in a new study.
story: Alzheimer's Association VP Rachel Conant joins 'Fox News Live' to discuss policy hurdles blocking access to breakthrough Alzheimer's treatments.
Many older adults turn to glucosamine to manage aging joints, but for individuals with mild cognitive impairment, the supplement could be linked to faster progression to Alzheimer’s disease.

To investigate how glucosamine affects dementia risk and mortality, University of Florida researchers analyzed medical records of patients with mild cognitive impairment, tracked laboratory mouse models and examined healthy versus Alzheimer’s-affected human brains.
The study, which was published in Nature Metabolism, focused on glycosylation, a natural process where brain cells attach small chains of sugar to proteins.
7 NEW DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS REVEALED — INCLUDING ONE MILLIONS STRUGGLE WITH

"You can think of these sugar chains as the labels and fittings on a machine part — they help a protein fold correctly, get shipped to the right place in the cell and connect with its partners," senior author Ramon Sun, Ph.D., professor of biochemistry and molecular biology in the College of Medicine at University of Florida, told Fox News Digital. "The right amount is essential."
Many older adults turn to glucosamine to manage aging joints, but for individuals with mild cognitive impairment, the supplement could be linked to faster progression to Alzheimer’s disease. (iStock)
What is glucosamine?

"Glucosamine is a naturally occurring compound of sugar and an amino acid group that is a fundamental structural building block in the body," Neil Levin, senior nutrition education manager of Now, a manufacturer of glucosamine supplements in Illinois, told Fox News Digital.

Glucosamine is concentrated in cartilage, the connective tissue that cushions joints, and is a component of larger molecules that help give cartilage its strength, elasticity and ability to retain water, he added.
"Support for aging joints is the primary reason people take glucosamine as a dietary supplement," Levin said.
ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TESTS MAY PREDICT SYMPTOMS YEARS IN ADVANCE, BUT EXPERTS URGE CAUTION
The body uses an internal "checkpoint" that naturally regulates how many of these sugar chains it produces, according to Sun.

Supplemental glucosamine bypasses that "front gate" entirely — like a delivery truck pulling straight up to the loading dock, instantly boosting the supply of raw material used to make the sugar chains, the expert added.

Glucosamine is concentrated in cartilage, the connective tissue that cushions joints, and is a component of larger molecules that help give cartilage its strength, elasticity and ability to retain water. (iStock)

In the study, researchers analyzed thousands of patients with dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, as well as those with mild cognitive impairment, and then narrowed the group to those who were taking glucosamine.

For those with mild cognitive impairment, taking the supplement didn't change their risk of death, but it did make them 25% more likely to progress to dementia. However, among individuals who already had dementia, glucosamine users had a higher mortality compared to similar non-users.
POPULAR DRUGS FOR BONE HEALTH LINKED TO SIGNIFICANTLY LOWER ALZHEIMER'S RISK
The researchers also examined brain tissue to understand what might be driving the association. "We found an excess of sugar chains on proteins in the Alzheimer’s brain," Sun said.

Many of those proteins help nerve cells communicate, but the excess sugar chains may interfere with how they function, Sun said. He compared the effect to coating a key in too much wax — it is still the same key, but no longer fits the lock properly.
"A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both."
Glucosamine is one of the materials cells use to make these sugar chains, according to Sun.
Researchers also tracked how glucosamine was processed in mice, comparing its effects on healthy brains with those affected by Alzheimer’s-like disease.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In our experiments, normal mice given glucosamine showed no increase in these sugar chains and no change in a memory test," Sun said.
"But in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease, where the production line was already running too hot, glucosamine increased the sugar chains further and worsened performance on a memory test."
Study limitations
The researchers relied on medical records, which may not capture every supplement a patient was taking.

"Health records tell us what was documented, not everything a person took," Sun said. "Over-the-counter supplements are not always recorded, and records don't reliably capture dose, brand or how consistently someone took it."

Researchers analyzed thousands of patients with dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, as well as those with mild cognitive impairment, and then narrowed the group to those who were taking glucosamine. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci, File)
An observational study looking at past records can find a signal, but can't prove one.

Glucosamine users may also differ in factors such as arthritis, pain, mobility, frailty and medication use, Levin noted. The records also did not establish the exact supplement, dose, duration or consistency of use.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The finding should therefore be treated as a safety signal that warrants controlled human research, but it did not — could not — reach a conclusion that glucosamine causes Alzheimer’s disease," Levin said.
The next step is a well-designed, double-blind clinical trial to evaluate the impact of glucosamine on cognitive decline in patients with dementia.
The study did not examine cognitively healthy people and does not suggest glucosamine poses a risk to those who take it for joint health. (iStock)

"For now, the evidence isn't strong enough to recommend any supplement for slowing [Alzheimer’s] disease, which is why doing this research properly, including the clinical trial we've called for, matters," Sun said.
The study did not examine cognitively healthy people and does not suggest that glucosamine poses a risk to those who take it for joint health.

"A brain affected by dementia and a healthy brain are different biological environments, and we shouldn't assume a supplement behaves the same way in both," Sun said.
He emphasized the importance of consulting with a doctor before starting or stopping a supplement.

"If you or a family member has a diagnosis of cognitive impairment or dementia and takes glucosamine, it's reasonable to bring it up at the next visit, as part of an ordinary conversation about what's in the medicine cabinet," the doctor advised.
