Rush had worked on secret maritime programs at the Pentagon, NBC News reported in June. Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg was interviewed by the FBI as part of the investigation into Rush; Feinberg has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the bureau said in a statement that he was not under investigation. There’s no indication Feinberg knew about Rush’s alleged fabrications. Several senior CIA officials were placed on leave over the management of Rush’s requests for money, NBC News reported in June.

The U.S. intelligence community’s inspector general is also investigating the circumstances that led to Rush’s arrest, which has raised questions among intelligence officials and U.S. lawmakers about how the CIA could have missed basic alleged falsehoods in Rush’s application, including about his academic and military records, NBC News reported last month.

title: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas
summary: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed on his way to work by ICE agents, who said he used his vehicle as a weapon. The community is demanding justice.
story: HOUSTON — As the sun set on a late September evening, a voice rose over the din of traffic at the roadside memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father fatally shot here by immigration authorities three months ago.
Sitting on barbershop steps, Berta Lopez, a nearby resident, alternately sang, recited prayers and cried for a man she never met.

“It was unjust — he was killed unjustly! The family is deeply hurt, his wife, his children. They are like family to us. And why don’t they show the people who did the killing? Why don’t they show them? Why don’t they release the names of the people who killed Lorenzo? Why don’t they expose them?” she said in Spanish.

In tears, Lopez said that after more than a year of intensive operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Salgado Araujo’s killing was a clarifying moment. The government, she said, saw those who weren’t U.S. citizens as less than nothing. She was tired of it.

“Just because we’re Hispanic, shouldn’t we hold our heads high? No, God doesn’t want us hanging our heads in shame. He wants all of us, his children, to hold our heads up high,” Lopez said. “God doesn’t care about papers.”

Lopez’s hurt and anger were reflected in NBC News interviews with more than three dozen Houston-area Latinos, elected officials, activists and political strategists. They reveal a distraught community whose members feel degraded by the messages they hear out of Washington, D.C., during President Donald Trump’s second term. They said they have been terrorized by the constant stories of those detained, many wrongly, and left to languish. They were aghast that the government was sending immigrants to countries they had never heard of.

Many said Salgado Araujo’s shooting death crystallized their feelings of powerlessness. Most Latinos were better versed in the details of the incident than in the names and backgrounds of those running for some of the highest-profile offices in their state.
Their refrains were in the same vein: That could have been my dad, my brother, my uncle, my son — or me.

title: Police knew who her rapist was. The law kept them from prosecuting him for the attack.
summary: After a certain point in some states, there’s no way to hold a perpetrator accountable for sexual assaults.
story: Dana Beatty survived a horrific rape that took decades to solve.

After 34 years, authorities were finally able to identify the masked intruder who pressed a knife to her neck, wrapped her face in tape, lashed her to a bed and assaulted her for hours on Aug. 1, 1989. DNA evidence pointed to a local doctor who turned out to be someone Beatty knew. He was the husband of her best friend.

But Beatty’s assailant couldn’t be charged with rape. Authorities told her that the statute of limitations for the crime — which was six years in Ohio at the time of the assault — had long since run out, and a 2015 update to the state’s statute didn’t revive the case.
“Disbelief” is how Beatty, 67, described her reaction to the development.
“I do not understand why there would even be a statute of limitations,” she told “Dateline” in her first interview about the issue. “I don’t understand what the value in that is.”

What happened to Beatty highlights an issue faced by adult survivors of sexual violence across the country: More than 30 states have statutes of limitations for the most serious charges of sexual assault — a crime that is generally described as rape but is prosecuted under different names in different states, according to data gathered this year by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit that tracks the issue and advocates for victims.

The data, which was verified and analyzed by NBC News, shows that time limits vary dramatically from state to state. Some states impose statutes of limitations of a decade or less with few exceptions, while others eliminate time limits entirely in some circumstances.
Calls for change
Several legal experts and advocates believe statutes of limitations for all or many such types of assaults should be eliminated.
Ayesha Bell Hardaway, a former prosecutor who is a professor of law at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio, is alarmed by the dramatic variation across the country.

“It should cause anyone to have some concern about whether or not there would be accountability,” she said. “If you have individuals who are able to perpetrate crimes in the ‘right’ location, where if you get past six years of looking over your shoulder there’s no way you would be held accountable, that is quite alarming.”

To Stefan Turkheimer, vice president of public policy with RAINN, the variations can leave survivors agonizing over “math problems” instead of seeking justice or dealing with the aftermath of a crime that has devastating consequences.

“They should be able to concentrate on their own healing rather than a race to the courthouse to see whether or not the doors will be locked for them,” he said. “It is an unfair situation that when so many survivors come forward, they find that the time limit for justice has expired and that there’s nothing that they can do and that this person that harmed them will continue to go free.”

Beatty immediately reported the rape to authorities, and investigators spent years trying to solve the crime. They even investigated a local police officer who early on was considered a potential suspect, according to Charlie Beaver, a former Cincinnati police detective.
But that officer had a “perfect” alibi, Beaver said, and investigators were unable to identify her attacker.

Margaret Drew, an associate professor of law at the University of Massachusetts who specializes in gender violence, said it’s not unusual for survivors to take years to report what happened to them. She said she was struck by the “ambivalence” some legislatures display about rape survivors through statutes of limitations.

“We now know that sexual assault is a significant, life-changing event for the survivors and has serious psychological and physical consequences,” she said. “Why doesn’t everyone just agree to remove the statute of limitations?”

In interviews with NBC News, legal experts and advocates echoed that point. Some said there should be no time limits on any case involving nonconsensual sex; Hardaway said they should be eliminated for the most severe sexual assault charges, which can include the use of force or the threat of force or cases in which victims are incapacitated.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

But Nathan Rouse, an assistant professor of law at the University of South Carolina, cautioned that statutes of limitations act as deadlines for authorities to act on allegations. That can be crucial, he said, because investigations and prosecutions have historically been “sluggish, delayed or fully abandoned” for those victims.
“Discarding deadlines altogether is not a way to incentivize timely prosecutions of sexual assault cases,” he said.
Factoring in DNA evidence

Some who support eliminating time limits pointed to DNA evidence as a crucial tool that has transformed investigations and prosecutions. DNA, they said, can blunt evidentiary issues like faded memories, unavailable witnesses or lost evidence.

Such issues — along with what Turkheimer described as “court efficiency” — are the reasons statutes of limitations exist, they said. But no state has a time limit on the most serious crime, murder. And most states have eliminated them for certain sexual assault crimes involving children, according to Turkheimer.

Renee Williams, CEO of the National Center for Victims of Crime, said, “I don’t know why most states would not say, if there’s DNA, it blows the statute of limitations out of the water” for sexual assault prosecutions.

While nearly a dozen states eliminate time limits if DNA evidence is used to identify a suspect, six offer limited extensions of five years or less. In Iowa, the statute of limitations for the most serious rape charge — first-degree sexual abuse — is 10 years. An extra three years can get added if DNA evidence comes into play.

In Montana, the statute of limitations for aggravated sexual intercourse without consent — that state’s most serious rape charge — is five years, with a one-year DNA extension. The time limit is 10 years for the lesser crime of sexual intercourse without consent.

According to the Legislative Services Division of Montana’s Legislature, lawmakers created the aggravated charge in 2017 but never addressed the crime’s statute of limitations in committee hearings. It isn’t clear why. But the time limit automatically became five years — the “catchall” period for most felony crimes in the state, according to the division.

Seven other states and Washington, D.C., have statutes of limitations of 10 years or less and no DNA exceptions that extend the clock. In some states, these charges are misdemeanors or lower-level felonies. But in North Dakota, one of the most serious sex crimes has a time limit of seven years that can be paused only if the accused isn’t a resident of the state.
Such “tolling” provisions are common in state statutes. They pause the time limit in certain circumstances and often apply to all felony crimes.
Question of justice, not math

In Ohio, authorities initially believed they could pursue a rape charge against the man who assaulted Beatty, according to Jeff Smallwood, a Cincinnati police detective. While the statute of limitations for the crime was just six years in 1989, it was extended to 20 years in 1999, then again to 25 years with an additional five-year extension for DNA evidence in 2015.

When Smallwood approached the prosecutor’s office, he recalled, they believed that even though they were outside the 25-year window, the five-year DNA extension would kick in because of biological evidence recovered from Beatty’s dress.

Using genetic genealogy, the investigators determined the DNA was that of Frederick Tanzer, a doctor who in 1989 was the husband of Beatty’s best friend. Authorities were preparing to make an arrest, Smallwood said, when the prosecutor’s office came back with bad news.
A misreading of the law meant that because the original statute of limitations had already run out, the DNA extension didn’t apply.
“They say, ‘We made a mistake,’” Smallwood recalled. “‘We are unable to prosecute this case.’”

A spokeswoman for the Hamilton County Prosecutor’s Office said the attorney who now leads the office wasn’t involved in the process, so it’s “impossible” to know how it unfolded. Turkheimer said the apparent mistake illustrates how the complexities of statutes of limitations can undermine the fundamental premise of the justice system.
“The reality is these should be questions of justice, but they’re often complicated math problems,” he said.

Because investigators in Ohio couldn’t pursue a rape charge, they reached out to federal authorities for help. Using a coffee cup that Tanzer threw out, the investigators confirmed Tanzer’s DNA was found on Beatty’s dress. And they began examining other possible crimes that Tanzer could be charged with, including allegations that he’d drugged his ex-wife and had nonconsensual sex with her, federal prosecutors wrote in a pretrial detention filing.

But those, too, were ruled out because, at the time of the alleged assaults, there was an exemption in Ohio law that barred spouses from being prosecuted for rape. (In an interview with “Dateline,” Tanzer declined to discuss the allegations.)
Such spousal exemptions once existed in every state, but few remain, Turkheimer said. Ohio eliminated its spousal rape exemption in 2024.
Last-ditch plan for prosecution
Authorities next developed what Smallwood described as a last-ditch plan to prosecute Tanzer — a ruse that could catch him lying about the rape. Then, he could be prosecuted for that lie.

After having made up a story about how authorities were investigating a police officer suspected of raping Beatty and covering it up, Smallwood said, they planned to approach Tanzer not as a suspect, but as a witness. They’d ask whether he knew anything about the attack.
The tricky part, said Julie D. Garcia, a federal prosecutor in Ohio’s Southern District, is that Tanzer could have refused.
“Everyone has a right to remain silent,” Garcia said. “And he would have been well within his rights to say: ‘I don’t want to talk to you. Close the door.’”
But Tanzer talked. And he lied.

He told them he didn’t speak with Beatty on Aug. 1, 1989, nor did he go to her apartment or have sex with her, a recording of the interview shows. On Dec. 11, 2024, Tanzer was arrested on suspicion of making false statements to a federal agent, and he later pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to 15 years in prison this year.
In the interview with “Dateline,” he admitted raping Beatty and said he was “working on the why.”

To Hardaway, the former prosecutor, authorities did the best they could in bringing the federal charges. But the case, she said, was the “perfect example” of why statutes of limitations shouldn’t apply to a crime like rape — especially when the suspect’s identity is unknown.

“These types of crimes have an enormous impact on those who are not able to protect themselves,” she said. “To be in a place where there isn’t a recognition of that from the legislatures and a more uniform approach to sexual assault crimes, I think, is very telling about the priorities of our nation.”
For Beatty, eliminating statutes of limitations wouldn’t just deliver the appropriate punishment to criminals, she said.
“To me, that would be relief,” she said. “True relief.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

title: Where you live matters when it comes to prosecuting rape suspects
summary: A murderer can be convicted decades after committing the crime, because there is no statute of limitations on most homicides in America.
story: A murderer can be convicted decades after committing the crime, because there is no statute of limitations on most homicides in America.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The same isn’t always true for sexual assault, as Dana Beatty learned when DNA evidence pointed to a suspect 34 years after her brutal assault, because under Ohio law, time was up.

The statute of limitations for the most serious sexual assault cases can vary significantly for American adults depending on what state they live in, according to 2026 data from the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit that tracks the issue. NBC News verified and analyzed the data.

title: Trump uses anti-trans slur against Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina
summary: Annie Andrews is a physician running against Sen. Darline Graham.
story: President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Darline Graham.
In a Truth Social post, Trump referred to Democratic candidate Annie Andrews three times as “trannie.” He said Andrews, who is not transgender, is “not for South Carolina.”
“And South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her,” Trump added.
Andrews responded by largely ignoring the insult, saying in a statement first shared with NBC News that she will “work with anyone to put South Carolina first.”

“As a mom and a pediatrician, I’m in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids, and South Carolina,” Andrews said, adding that “lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together.”
“If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said.
Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the post by Trump, who often uses insulting nicknames for politicians and officials he dislikes.
Reached for comment on why Trump used the slur, the White House referred NBC News to his social media post.
The Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ advocacy organization, blasted Trump’s remarks, calling them “the sad, disgusting, pathetic diatribes of a lame duck president with record-low approvals.”

“So low, in fact, he’s having to campaign in deep red territory in a desperate attempt to shore up support ahead of the midterms,” Ramiro Sarmiento, a spokesperson for the organization, said in a statement.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., condemned Trump’s words Monday night, calling his attacks on Andrews “despicable.”
“Annie Andrews is a mom and pediatrician who’s always put her community first — and she’s exactly who South Carolina needs representing them in the Senate,” Schumer said on X.
Andrews, a physician, has previously said she does not support gender-affirming surgery for minors or transgender athletes’ participating in women’s sports.
Graham is running to keep her seat after Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fill her late brother’s seat after Lindsey Graham died in July.
Graham won the Republican primary in a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman by nearly 5 percentage points. She has leaned heavily on Trump’s endorsement to make her case to South Carolina.

While South Carolina has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly three decades, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race toward Democrats last month, moving it from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”

title: After bipartisan criticism, Trump says taxpayers’ dollars will no longer be used for TV ads promoting him
summary: The president said the ads, which the White House has defended, will be funded by him and his super PAC, MAGA Inc.
story: In a major reversal, President Donald Trump said Monday that he and his super PAC will now pay for campaign-style ads that promote his administration, instead of using federal funds.
Trump made the announcement on Truth Social after intense criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, some of whom questioned the legality of using taxpayer dollars for pro-Trump ads.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., did not immediately respond to an inquiry about whether Trump and it would reimburse the government for the ads that have already aired. The White House did not answer that question, either.
“MAGA Inc. will pay for the PSA ads moving forward,” a White House official said.

“Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction,” the official added.
AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated the government has spent at least $10 million to air the ads.
The ads, which portray Trump in a favorable light, included disclaimers saying they were paid for by the U.S. government. One of the spots was virtually identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
NBC News reported last week that the ads were paid for by money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, but senior leaders at the agency were cut out of the decision.
A Maryland-based firm, LMD Agency, was awarded a $20 million contract for the new ads, according to public contracting records. The purpose of the contract was listed as a “national media campaign.”

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have condemned the ads. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it “propaganda,” while Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, likened Trump to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán.
“There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said.

The White House previously defended the ads, calling them “clearly not political” and saying the PSAs were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

title: 3 takeaways from our new poll of Latino voters: From the Politics Desk
summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
story: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Scott Bland breaks down the key numbers to know from our new national poll of the Latino electorate. Plus, Sahil Kapur dives into Democrats’ lingering divisions over transgender issues.
— Adam Wollner
3 takeaways from our new poll of  Latino voters
Latino voters’ swing toward President Donald Trump was one of the defining trends of the 2024 election. Their swing back could define the 2026 midterms, too.

That’s the broad takeaway from the NBC News/Telemundo poll that came out Sunday, which showed Democrats with a 24-point lead among Latino registered voters on a 2026 ballot test. That’s a double-digit turnaround from the 2024 edition of the survey — and it comes after Republicans in Florida and Texas made big redistricting bets on extending the party’s results in the last election.
Here are three big takeaways from the numbers:

The economy is the driving factor. Immigration and border security are still important to many Latino voters, but their top issue is the cost of living, and Trump’s inability to follow through on his campaign promise to lower prices is biting his party. Latino voters gave Trump a 4-percentage-point edge over Kamala Harris in 2024 on who they thought would do a better job handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.
That’s a big reason almost a quarter (22%) of Latino Trump voters said they’re not planning to back Republicans in the midterms, with 14% choosing Democrats and 8% undecided from that group.

Visceral feelings on immigration. Again, it’s not a leading issue when voters have to rank them, but Latino voters have strong feelings about Trump’s immigration agenda. Two-thirds say his enforcement policies have gone too far. Only 39% approve of his handling of border security and 30% approve on immigration overall.

Meanwhile, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying ID because of concerns about getting swept up by ICE enforcement operations, and 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE since Trump’s second term began.

There were key differences across gender, region and more. Just like in the overall electorate, Latino women lean more Democratic than Latino men. And while the sample was small, Latino voters from Florida were less likely to back Democrats than Latino voters elsewhere — something to keep in mind on election night, when it would be unwise to expect uniform swings from 2024 across different regions.
➡️ Related read: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas, by Natasha Korecki
Trump-district Democrats draw blowback from Human Rights Campaign over trans rhetoric

The country’s largest LGBTQ rights group is criticizing some Democrats who are adopting what they see as anti-transgender rhetoric in their campaigns, a point of tension as the party wrestles with how to handle the issue heading into the 2026 election.

They include Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, who said in a recent ad, “I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports.”
For Subscribers

They also include Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., who is similarly running in a red-leaning district that Donald Trump carried in the last election. In a recent ad, Davis cited a North Carolina law that prohibits trans women and girls from playing on female sports teams, saying there are “real concerns about fairness and safety” for “women and girls in sports.”
Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson told reporters today that those candidates are “doing too much and getting too little” with their strategies.
For Subscribers
“You don’t have to sacrifice any member of our community to win in these races, to have a message that resonates with voters,” Robinson said at a breakfast in Washington.

“You’ve got Marcy Kaptur, who not only is bad on the message, but she’s also bad on the policy. I mean, she voted for a bill that would have put forced outing in place nationally. A don’t-say-trans bill, too, right? She’s somebody that hasn’t been with us on either of those sides, so she’s not someone that we’re supporting this cycle,” Robinson said.

Meanwhile, Robinson praised former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who is running again for the Senate in Ohio. Brown has sought to reframe the debate, featuring a voter in an ad who says: “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?”

“Sherrod Brown, on the other hand, I think, did a great job in his response ad that we worked with him pretty closely on — in stating what the laws are in Ohio now and reaffirming his support from the community and then, most importantly, letting voters talk for themselves,” Robinson said.

In light of the criticism, Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer said in a statement: “Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls’ sports stay fair. She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor.”
A Davis spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has not advised 2026 candidates to take any particular approach on trans issues, according to a person familiar with the committee’s thinking, who said it is “supportive of each candidate messaging as they see fit” in their districts while simply encouraging them to “explain to voters where they stand.”
Where the Human Rights Campaign and the Democrats they are criticizing agree is that the GOP attacks are effective if left unanswered. But they disagree over how to answer them.

Robinson argued that the “core failure” of Democrats and Kamala Harris in 2024 was “the lack of a direct response.” She said of 2026: “We’ve given counsel and guidance that’s really very clear. Address the attack head-on, pivot to your values — the things that you want voters to know about.”

A Democratic strategist involved in 2026 races said that is one school of thought, which can be effective in message testing. Another school of thought, said the strategist, is to directly confront the attacks and seek distance on the issue in order to “not look like a typical Democrat.”
The latter approach “works better as your district gets redder,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to discuss internal machinations on the record.

title: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is the country’s largest in three decades
summary: More than 1,000 people have been infected and nearly 200 have been hospitalized as the state struggles to contain the spread of the extremely infectious disease.
story: Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak is now the largest in the U.S. in three decades. On Monday, the state surpassed South Carolina’s outbreak earlier this year, which topped out at 997.
That outbreak was contained within six months. Pennsylvania’s outbreak, which began in late April, shows no sign of slowing.

“I would bet that this goes on for at least another three to six months,” said Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease expert at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center. “We have seen an increase in vaccinations, but we aren’t seeing enough people get vaccinated to stop the epidemic.”
On Monday, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported 1,004 measles cases, with 198 hospitalizations. Nearly a third of the cases have been in children.

Among the pediatric measles cases, 18% have needed hospitalization. Dehydration has become a common problem, particularly among babies and younger children, said Dr. Evan Shirey, a pediatric infectious disease physician at Penn State Health Golisano Children’s Hospital in Hershey.
Doctors are also seeing young patients with liver problems.

“One of the more common things that the measles virus can do is cause hepatitis or infection of the liver,” Shirey said. “These children will feel very sick, very nauseous, with abdominal pain and vomiting, and they can’t take a bottle or can’t keep food or liquid down.”

Other children are developing severe and irreversible neurological damage because of brain inflammation, or encephalitis, Shirey said. “In some of these cases, it’s a child who can’t recognize their own mother, who’s disoriented and confused,” Shirey said. Still others have developed secondary bacterial infections.

Five people in the state have died, according to the health department. Those people include a teenager with severe brain inflammation and a 40-year-old woman with a history of asthma, as well as two babies. One of those babies was a newborn who died after his mother went into labor a month early.
There are few details about the fifth person who died, other than the person hadn’t been vaccinated and lived in Lancaster County, where the bulk of measles cases are.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Lancaster County is home to the nation’s largest Amish population, with approximately 44,000 residents as of 2025. There is nothing in the religion that is inherently anti-vaccine, but historically, their vaccination rates have been lower than those of the general population, Goldman said.

According to an NBC News investigation, 88.5% of kindergartners in 2024 had the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. A vaccination rate of at least 95% is the accepted level of herd immunity needed to protect against a measles outbreak.

“There’s nothing special about Lancaster. The exact same thing could happen in any county in the country that has a large percentage of unvaccinated people,” Goldman said. “If it hasn’t happened yet, it’s only because measles hasn’t gotten into that county yet.”

The outbreak in South Carolina, which ended in April, was previously the largest in approximately 30 years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That outbreak was linked to a community of people who emigrated from Ukraine over the past few decades. State health officials credited a massive surge in vaccinations with bringing the outbreak to a halt.

In the northwestern corner of the state, where the outbreak was centered, nearly 15,000 MMR vaccinations were given during the South Carolina outbreak, up 82% compared with the previous year, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Health.
As of Monday, the Pennsylvania health department said it’s given just 8,843 MMR doses so far in response to the outbreak.

Ohio is also dealing with a growing measles outbreak along the border it shares with Pennsylvania. As of Thursday, Ohio had logged 210 measles cases, with 13 hospitalizations. Most cases are concentrated in the northeastern part of the state, in Geauga, Ashtabula and Wayne counties.

title: Chicago woman shot 5 times by CBP officer files federal lawsuit
summary: Attorneys for Marimar Martinez alleged a new analysis of the bullets’ trajectories shows Border Patrol Agent Charles Exum wasn’t in front of her vehicle and the last shot went through the rear passenger seat.
story: A woman who survived being shot five times by a Border Patrol agent in Chicago filed a federal civil lawsuit Monday against the U.S. government as her attorneys allege that new evidence shows the agent was not in danger for his life and should face criminal charges.

Marimar Martinez, a teaching aide at a Montessori school, was shot in her car by Customs and Border Protection agent Charles Exum in October. The shooting occurred during the Trump administration’s mass immigration enforcement surge in Chicago last year, known as Operation Midway Blitz.

The lawsuit was filed a year after Martinez was shot under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows private citizens to sue the federal government. Federal agents cannot be directly sued, the attorneys said.

The lawsuit alleges negligence, battery, assault, intentional infliction of emotional distress, false arrests, false imprisonment and malicious prosecution, attorney Michael Gallagher said at a news conference Monday.
“The reality is the shoot wasn’t justified. She almost lost her life as a result. She’s been dealing with the physical and mental injuries ever since then,” he said.
The attorneys also urged the Justice Department and local prosecutors to file criminal charges against Exum.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that consistent with policy, Exum was placed on administrative leave, though it did not immediately say whether Exum is still on leave. DHS referred all other questions to the Justice Department, which declined to comment on ongoing litigation.
For Subscribers

According to Christopher Parente, also an attorney for Martinez, the investigation and an analysis of the scene his firm commissioned showed that Border Patrol agent Charles Exum shot Martinez without justification and was not in danger at the time of the shooting.

The attorneys showed a visual reconstruction alleging where Exum would have been standing as he opened fire on Martinez based on the bullets’ markings in her vehicle, her wounds and surveillance video.

Martinez was not driving at Exum when he shot her five times, as he had previously claimed, the attorneys said. One of the bullets, they alleged, went through the side of the rear passenger-side car seat, which showed Exum could not have been standing in front of the car when he shot.
“He was in no way, shape or form in the path of the vehicle. She was actually driving away from him, and we established that he charged her,” Gallagher said.
For Subscribers
Exum was not wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting. In August, DHS said all ICE officers and agents in the field would be required to wear body cameras.
Martinez spoke briefly at the news conference, saying, “Right now, we’re just focused on moving forward with the civil case and just heal emotionally and physically.”
“I’m just glad to see another year, be with my family,” she said. “I want to spread awareness, because what’s happening is not normal. We shouldn’t stay here and normalize what’s happening.”

After the shooting, Martinez and another person at the scene were charged with using their vehicles to attempt to ram federal law enforcement officers, but the charges were dropped after federal prosecutors filed a motion to dismiss their own case. The motion came after additional video of the incident was shown and after it was revealed that Exum had bragged about the shooting in messages to other officers.
According to Reuters, records presented at the hearing showed that in a group Signal chat with other agents, Exum wrote: “I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys.”
In a message to another recipient, Exum sent a news article about the event followed by the message: “Read it. 5 shots, 7 holes,” Reuters reported.
Parente asked Exum what he meant by those messages at the time. According to records presented at a hearing, Exum responded: “I’m a firearms instructor and I take pride in my shooting skills.”
Martinez’s case has been one of the highest-profile examples of federal authorities accusing civilians of ramming into vehicles driven by immigration agents.

title: White House removes Politico from press pool for Trump’s trip to Nebraska
summary: The administration took similar action last week against CNN. The cable news network, MS NOW and Politico sued after they were banned from the White House grounds.
story: The White House prohibited Politico on Monday from traveling on Air Force One with President Donald Trump as he heads to Nebraska for a campaign rally.
The move comes amid a legal fight between the Trump administration and several news organizations.

“Many outlets including Politico are granted access to attend and cover presidential events unilaterally, but traveling with the President of the United States aboard Air Force One is a privilege not a right,” a White House official said in a statement.
CNN first reported the administration’s action against Politico.

The White House last month banned Politico, CNN and MS NOW from entering the White House, with Trump saying on Truth Social that the move was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” A federal judge last month ordered the administration to temporarily restore their access, but the order was limited to the White House grounds.

Dana Beckman, a spokesperson for Politico, confirmed that the news outlet was excluded from the travel pool but did not have additional comment. A lawyer representing the three news outlets in their lawsuit against the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The White House last week removed CNN from the press pool set to cover Trump’s trip to Texas and Oklahoma.

The White House press pool consists of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps each day to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The White House press corps has separate print, radio, still photography and TV pools.

Politico was set to serve as the print travel pool Monday. A pool note from CBS News, which is handling the TV pool for the day, said the White House was unable to find a news outlet to replace Politico.

After CNN was restricted from administration events last month, the four other member networks of the press pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — declined to participate in pool duties in solidarity.

CBS on Monday said it would share its TV pool notes — which are usually distributed internally among the five pool networks — with the White House Correspondents’ Association. The network noted it was not replacing Politico as the print pool.

The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last month in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

title: Ex-‘American Idol’ contestant Caleb Flynn sentenced to life without parole in wife’s murder
summary: The “American Idol” contestant and music pastor was found guilty last week in the shooting death of his wife in their Ohio home.
story: A former Ohio music pastor and “American Idol” contestant has been sentenced to life without possibility of parole for killing his wife in their Dayton-area home earlier this year.
Caleb Flynn, 40, was found guilty of aggravated murder in the February shooting of Ashley Flynn, 37, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach. Flynn and their two daughters were home when police arrived.
Before issuing the sentence, Judge Jeannine Pratt said he would be punished because he posed a high risk of harm to the community.
“The layers of deceit, manipulation and cruelty are hard to fathom,” Pratt said Monday. “And you used your faith to manipulate the lives of others.”
Flynn maintained his innocence Monday, crying and shaking as he read a statement to his family and Ashley’s.

“I loved her and loved her. She was my wife. She was beautiful and amazing in countless ways,” Flynn said. “I will continue to fight for my innocence as long as the Lord allows me to, since I did not kill my wife.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
To his two children, Flynn apologized and said they are his greatest joy in life. He thanked his parents for their love and kindness and said their support throughout the trial was “supernatural.”

“I never knew that love this fierce was possible until the moment that I held you for the first time,” Flynn said to his daughters. “Please know your daddy is so proud of you and loves you beyond what words can describe.”
Flynn’s daughters were not in court, but other family members read written statements from the preteen girls who were ages 9 and 11 when their mother was killed.
“I love you deeply with all my heart and it’s sad that you can’t love anyone but yourself,” read the letter from his daughter Alissa.
In her letter, his daughter Ava said photos and videos of her father on trial online have been inescapable.
“My heart aches to see you hurt, but then I think it was your choice,” she wrote. “It was your choice to have that affair.”

Both daughters implored their father to confess to murdering their mother. Along with their grandparents, uncle and aunt, who read statements in court, the girls said their faith has been helping them get through their grief.

Ashley Flynn’s sister, Kayla Keyt, said during her victim statement that her family could not overcome their sense of shock and despair after learning that Flynn betrayed them in such a violent and horrible way.
“We trusted you. We believed in you. We honestly would have laid down our lives for you,” Keyt said.
Prosecutors said Flynn’s wife was defenseless in bed when he shot her and then feigned a home invasion to mislead investigators.
Flynn frantically called 911 and said someone had broken in while he slept on the couch. He woke up to the sound of gunshots, he told investigators.
He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”

But Flynn’s lover, Alleigha Botner, testified in court that he talked about hating his wife and having thoughts of killing her. Jurors heard AI-generated love songs that prosecutors say he made for Botner and some of the more than 100,000 text messages that authorities say they exchanged.
Miami County Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins read a statement to the court and shook his head as prosecutors said he endangered his children’s lives when he killed his wife while they were home.
“This case is about deliberate choices, the destruction of an irreplaceable life and the permanent devastation left behind,” he said.
“The defendant has never accepted responsibility or expressed genuine remorse for the life he ended,” Watkins added.

title: NFL suspends two referees for ‘unprofessional conduct’ toward players
summary: Line judge Jeff Seeman will miss two games and referee Adrian Hill will miss one for altercations during Sunday’s games.
story: Two NFL officials whose behavior toward players drew scrutiny Sunday have been sidelined by the league.
The NFL said Monday it has suspended line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one after contentious interactions with players in different games during Week 4.
The suspensions were handed down by the NFL’s vice president of officiating, Ramon George, and each was issued because of “an instance of unprofessional conduct toward a player,” the league said.
Representatives for the unions representing NFL players and referees did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
More from Sports

Arizona Cardinals tight end Trey McBride was coming off the field during the fourth quarter of Sunday’s game against the New York Giants when a sideline camera showed Seeman appearing to use profanity toward him.

JC Tretter, the executive director of the NFL Players Association, singled out the play as “unacceptable” Sunday on X. “Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard.”

During the Minnesota Vikings’ victory against the Miami Dolphins, Hill was knocked over when a first-quarter play was whistled dead but Miami running back Ollie Gordon continued to block Minnesota’s Eric Wilson into Hill. Hill stood up and yelled at Wilson.
After the game, Wilson told reporters that he and Hill had spoken about the exchange.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“I ended up apologizing to him and explained the situation,” Wilson said. “He was cool about it. He understood what was going on. He just said he didn’t want us fighting.”
Seeman has been an NFL official since 2002, while Hill started in 2010.

title: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
summary: The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.
story: The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.

The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

“While the circumstances of this reported case remain unconfirmed, plague is a serious bacterial disease that is treatable with antibiotics, particularly when recognized and treated early,” a spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. “At this time, there is no indication from available reporting of a broader threat to the United States.”

Key details aren’t known, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people who came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media.

“Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine.

Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.”
“We need to understand that now,” he added.
The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is.
What is plague?

Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics.
It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization. All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body.

Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious.
Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said.
Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood.
How does pneumonic plague spread?
Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes.

The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.”
It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO.

Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said.
“It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said.
For Subscribers
Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet.
“It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said.
How deadly is it?
While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest.
For Subscribers
“It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said.

It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm.
Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici.

People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Healthcare workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure.
“We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said.
How is it treated?
Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague.
“This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said.

Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.”
Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.”
“The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said.
Is the plague found in the U.S.?

About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC. Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas.
Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen.

Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague.

title: DNA confirms body found in Texas creek is missing flight attendant
summary: The roommate of 47-year-old Rana Nofal Soluri has already been charged in connection with the death.
story: Prosecutors seeking to convict the Texas man charged with killing flight attendant Rana Nofal Soluri and throwing her body off a bridge have a powerful new piece of evidence — the victim’s body.
Soluri’s remains were found on June 13 but only recently have been “confirmed to be her through DNA testing,” a spokesperson for the Fort Worth Police Department told NBC News on Sunday.

Her body was found by a fisherman trolling beneath a bridge on the bank of a creek in Montague County, which is about 70 miles northwest of downtown Fort Worth, police told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram. The body was then taken to the University of North Texas Health’s Center for Human Identification.

It has since been released to her daughter, Lulu Soluri, according to a GoFundMe page set up on her behalf. American Airlines flew the body to Seattle for a Muslim burial that took place on Sept. 29, an update on the GoFundMe announced.
Soluri worked for a regional carrier owned by American Airlines.
The break in the case came more than a year after Soluri’s former roommate, 67-year-old Dennis Day, was arrested in June 2025 and charged with murder.
Police took Day into custody two months after the 47-year-old flight attendant went missing around March 19, 2025.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

A short time later, Joni Thomas, now 63 and also known as Joanne Walters, was accused of helping him dump Soluri’s body, police said. She was charged with tampering with evidence with intent to impair a human corpse.
Soluri had lived with Day for approximately a year, police said. She had taken some time off for a minor operation and was supposed to return to work on March 31, 2025.
When she didn’t, a co-worker reported her missing on June 11, 2025, police said.
Suspicion quickly fell on Day, who later admitted to police that he “snapped” during a dispute with Soluri before he “began to strangle her with his bare hands,” his arrest warrant said.

After the slaying, Day loaded Soluri’s body “head first, into a large black trash bin and transported” it 70 miles away to Bowie, a town in Montague County, where he dumped the remains over a bridge, according to the court document.
Day, police said, may have implicated himself and Thomas by accidentally recording themselves while transporting the victim’s body.
Investigators in September revealed they found an “inadvertent call” and message on Thomas’ phone on which a panicked Day can be heard asking for her help to move Soluri.
“This report is consistent with how Dennis Day stated that he moved [Soluri’s] body into a trash can and into the bed of a truck at his house,” Day’s arrest warrant said.

“This report also confirms the fact that not only did [Thomas] travel to [Day’s] house and allowed [Day] to use her truck to transport [Soluri’s] body, but that she actually helped load [Soluri’s] body into the truck.”
Investigators also found home security video from Day’s home, showing him dragging “what appears to be a lifeless body from the home into the backyard,” on March 21, police said.

It was not immediately clear where Day was being held. He had been listed as a prisoner at the Tarrant County Corrections Center. But his name did not come up Monday in a search of the prison’s online registry.

title: Some Democrats don’t expect to fill a Supreme Court vacancy under Trump
summary: Democrats need a net gain of four seats to capture the Senate. If they get it, they’d control what happens in a vacancy, as Justice Samuel Alito admits he has thought about retirement.
story: WASHINGTON — Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., is putting President Donald Trump on notice: If Democrats win control, they don’t intend to put “MAGA” judges on the courts.

“The bottom line is: One of the reasons we want to do everything we can to take back the Senate is not let Trump put such horrible justices — MAGA justices — on the Supreme Court and the lower courts,” Schumer said in response to a question from NBC News about a potential high court vacancy if Democrats win in 2026.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a senior member of the Judiciary Committee, said he doesn’t think a Democratic-led Senate would confirm a Trump pick for the Supreme Court either.

“Well, given the history of Trump nominees, I think it is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration,” Blumenthal said in an interview. “Because we’ve seen this movie, we know how it ends, which is a politician in robes who is following Trump’s orders on most major questions.”
Add to Google
Add to Google

The remarks highlight the high stakes of the 2026 election for Trump’s final two years when it comes to judicial nominees, especially for the Supreme Court if there’s a vacancy. None of the nine justices has signaled plans to retire, but speculation has centered on how long the two oldest justices — conservatives Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76 — will stay on the court. Justice Sonia Sotomayor and Chief Justice John Roberts are the next oldest justices, at 72 and 71, respectively.
Alito told CBS News in a recent interview that he considered retirement earlier this year, but ultimately decided against it.

“It’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term,” Alito said, while adding: “It’s too hard to predict what the political situation will be, and what any president might do with respect to a replacement.”

If Democrats win control of the Senate, they would have the power to determine which of Trump’s nominees for federal judicial postings get hearings and votes, including for a hypothetical Supreme Court vacancy.

But if Republicans keep control, the president will maintain his glide path to fill vacancies with his preferred nominees — adding to his nearly six-year total of 290 federal judges, including three Supreme Court justices during his first term. All of those judges have been confirmed under GOP Senate control.

Some Democrats say there should be no question of confirming a Trump pick after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., held a seat open for 10 months under President Barack Obama to let a Republican president fill it instead. (Justice Neil Gorsuch ultimately filled that vacancy.)
“No, we’ve got to do exactly what McConnell did to us,” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said.
Gallego said he doesn’t want it to become a rule that no president can get a nominee confirmed by a Senate run by the opposing party. But at minimum, he wants Democrats to “even the scales.”

Beyond that, “I don’t think you know you want to go down that road,” the first-term Arizona Democrat said. “But clearly you know McConnell and Trump used, I would say, their power, whatever you want to call it, to change the makeup of the courts. And I think we have to start moving it back.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., who sits on the Judiciary Committee, said he wouldn’t count on Trump getting any Supreme Court nominee through a Democratic-led Senate.

“I don’t think it would be impossible. You know, there’s a slim possibility, very slim possibility,” Kennedy said. “But there’s a possibility that somebody would confuse me with Brad Pitt. I mean, it’s possible, but it’s not likely.”
Kennedy, like most U.S. senators quoted in this article, spoke before Alito’s comments to CBS News were published.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who took her late brother Lindsey Graham’s seat on the Judiciary Committee when she was appointed to the Senate, reacted directly to Alito’s remarks and connected it to her 2026 campaign for a six-year term.

“Should Justice Alito choose to retire next year, a Republican-majority Senate will be needed to vote and hopefully confirm a Supreme Court nominee from President Trump,” Graham wrote on X. “If Democrats control the Senate, they will not even allow a vote. And if they allow a vote, they will defeat a Trump-nominated candidate regardless of their qualifications.”
For Subscribers
Another open question is how a Democratic majority would approach Trump judicial nominees for the lower courts.
For Subscribers

Blumenthal said that one of his litmus tests for Trump judicial nominees up and down the courts is that they must be able to correctly answer who won the 2020 election, a question that various Trump nominees have refused to engage on as the president persists with false claims that it was stolen from him.
“We’ll stop a lot of these totally unqualified, ideologically right-wing nominees who won’t answer the question of who won the 2020 election,” Blumenthal said. “Among other questions.”

Some Democrats with a long memory haven’t forgotten that McConnell slowed nearly all judicial nominations to a crawl in Obama’s last two years, when the Kentucky Republican first took charge as Senate majority leader. McConnell saw it as payback for Democrats abolishing the 60-vote threshold for lower court judges in 2013, which at the time was part of a rapidly escalating judicial war between the parties.
Still, not all Democrats are willing to speculate on how they would deal with Trump’s judicial nominees.
Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, another member of the Judiciary Committee, paused and chuckled when asked if Democrats would confirm a Trump-nominated justice to the Supreme Court.

“Well, I don’t know. I can’t speak for my colleagues,” she said. “Let us just say that I would be very much for Supreme Court reform. ... One that allows every president to nominate two Supreme Court justices, and then they move on” to senior status.

Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., the current ranking member of the Judiciary Committee, is retiring after this Congress. Next in line to chair the panel, should Democrats capture the Senate, would be Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.
Whitehouse declined to engage when asked what the dynamic of judicial nominations would be if he becomes chairman.
“Don’t know,” he said.
Josh Orton, the president of the progressive judicial group Demand Justice, said his organization is “prepared to oppose any Trump nominee, regardless of when the vacancy happens.”

“On moral and political grounds, I don’t see any reason for Democrats to consider a Trump Supreme Court nomination,” Orton said, adding that Trump wants judges to be personally loyal to him, and would select them on that basis. “Any casual observer knows that Trump sees the Supreme Court generally as a political extension of himself — or that it should be.”

Just last month, Trump issued a lengthy criticism of the Supreme Court on Truth Social for ruling against him on mail-in ballots, tariffs and birthright citizenship. “The Supreme Court has really let our Country down. ... These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court,” he wrote. “They are merely a shell of their original selves.”

CORRECTION (Oct. 5, 2026, 12:55 p.m. ET): Due to an editing error, a previous version of this article misstated who ultimately filled the Supreme Court vacancy that arose at the end of President Barack Obama’s term. It was Justice Neil Gorsuch, not Brett Kavanaugh.

title: Inspired by ‘90s Nostalgia and ‘Scooby-Doo’, The Lawrence Brothers Launch New Graphic Novel
summary: During a family vacation, the Lawrence brothers joked about starting a detective agency.
story: During a family vacation, the Lawrence brothers joked about starting a detective agency.

A guest at where they were vacationing had misplaced a valuable piece of jewelry while at the beach, Joey Lawrence tells TODAY.com. As the investigation continued, he, along with brothers Matt and Andrew Lawrence, began creating fictional storylines about finding the “lost treasure.” In one scenario, Matt even got a bad sunburn, before shedding his skin to reveal that he was the villain of the story. The ideas kept coming.

So after years of “fooling around with the idea,” the trio finally decided to team up with the Berkowitz Brothers, Ben and Max Berkowitz, Sean Von Gorman and Z2 to bring “The Lawrence Brothers Detective Agency,” an original graphic novel series, to life.

“The Lawrence Brothers Detective Agency” can best be described as a series about “three brothers whose knack for getting into trouble is only matched by their talent for solving mysteries,” Andy tells TODAY.com. “Every case brings clues, chaos, nostalgia, and the kind of brotherly love that only us Lawrence brothers can deliver.”
The siblings have a long history of collaborating on screen, starting with their 1995 sitcom “Brotherly Love,” along with “Horse Sense,” “Jumping Ship,” “Mistletoe Mixup” and more.
A graphic novel, on the other hand, is something new and creative for the trio.

“We’ve been throwing around this idea for years. We wanted to do sort of a grown up ‘Scooby-Doo’ meets ‘Hardy Boys’ and it just kind of came together,” Joey says. “We threw in some ‘90s nostalgia because it’s all the craze.”
Inspired by the Scooby Gang, in the first graphic novel they included nods to the franchise by including a mystery van and other “hidden Mickeys” that would make millennials nostalgic.
The first installment, out now, is the detective agency’s origin story.
“We love the fact that you can really take a lot of chances in this type of format, and that’s what we always loved about comic books and animated series,” Matt says.
Because they “know each other so well,” Andy says, their decadeslong working relationship just flows. Matt adds that when it comes to getting creative, they all come at it from very different angles.
“The sum of the three parts is always going to be better than us individually, in my opinion,” he says.
Calling this graphic novel among their most “unique” projects together, they first hoped to create an animated series.
“An adult ‘Scooby-Doo,’” Joey says, adding that they would “edge up the rating” for an older audience. “I feel like you could have so much fun with that.”
They aim to expand the universe with additional cases and, yes, one day create an animated series or perhaps a live-action show.
For now, Matt says, “Every novel that we put out would be a different case that we would take on. So at the end of this one, not to give too much away, we kind of say: We’re open for business.”

title: How ‘Sister Wives’ Stars Reacted to Kody Brown Not Being on the Show for the 1st Time in 16 Years
summary: Why is Kody Brown not on Sister Wives? How Christine, Janelle and Meri reacted to him not being on the show.
story: “Sister Wives” returned for Season 21 on Oct. 4 without its longtime star, Kody Brown.
For 16 years, the TLC series has followed as Kody and his four wives and their children navigated life in a plural marriage.

Brown and his only remaining wife, Robyn, left the series before filming for the new season began, forcing Kody Brown’s ex-wives  — Janelle, Christine and Meri —  to react to the couple’s exit on camera.

“I don’t know how to process it all. I’m just going to be honest. No idea how I feel about this whole thing,” Christine said in a confessional, adding, “ It’s just bizarre they’re done ... I don’t know what it means. I have no idea.”
In her own confessional, Janelle revealed she was “very shocked” to hear Kody and Robin would not be returning to the show.
Kody and Robin’s abrupt exit comes after years of upheaval in the family.
In 2021, Christine ended her spiritual marriage to Kody after 25 years and six children together.
Not long after, Janelle ended her union with Kody after nearly 30 years and six children.
Janelle and Kody also shared in the tragic loss of their son Garrison, who died in 2024.

Both Christine and Janelle went on to find love with new partners: In 2023, Christine tied the knot with David Woolley, and Janelle went public in August with a new boyfriend named Pete, who appears on “Sister Wives” this season.
Kody and Robin, who was originally his fourth wife, legally married in 2014 after Kody legally divorced Meri.
Already a mom of three, Robin went on to welcome two children, Solomon and Ariella, with Kody.
With feelings bitter among Kody and his exes by the end of Season 20, Kody vowed to do a “pilgrimage” to “apologize” to all three of the women.
The Season 21 premiere included footage from those apologies, which Janelle said Kody did to boost his image.

“I feel like the apology tour was, in the end, something he was trying to redeem himself with, and I don’t think it was necessarily that sincere because there’s been no contact since,” Janelle said in a confessional.

“He very publicly torpedoed my character afterwards, so I’m like, yeah, whatever,” Janelle added, addressing Kody’s public claim that Janelle tried to arrange deal with Kody to sell the family’s Coyote Pass property in Flagstaff, Arizona, behind Meri’s back.
“All of the sudden, here, months after the deal is closed, he starts talking about how I was doing this backdoor deal,” Janelle said. “I was like, ‘Where did that come from?’”
“I was not scheming. If I had been scheming, you would not have known it,” Janelle added.
Janelle described Kody’s public accusation as “a final f--- you” to her.
“It’d be one thing if he just said it, but everybody’s believing him,” said Janelle.
During the episode, Janelle asked Meri to meet with her in person so she could clear the air about what Kody said about the property deal.
“I’m frustrated that he wants to continue to stir up the drama. I don’t want to give him that kind of power,” Janelle told Meri.
“It got really way more complicated than it needed to be, and I don’t know why,” Janelle said, adding, “But, it’s done, and I was not trying to cut you out of a deal.”
The episode concluded by showing Janelle, Meri and Christine putting their tensions aside to reunite and sort through family photos together.
The news was confirmed in the Season 21 trailer in released in mid September, with a title card that said, “After 16 years of filming ‘Sister Wives,’ Kody & Robyn will not be returning to the show.”
TODAY.com has reached out to Kody and TLC for comment.

title: Aaron Sorkin Says Jeremy Strong Was in Character 24/7: ‘Never Heard Him Speak in His Own Voice’
summary: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in the new movie “The Social Reckoning” did not end when the cameras stopped filming for the day.
story: Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in the new movie “The Social Reckoning” did not end when the cameras stopped filming for the day.
Director Aaron Sorkin shared on TODAY Oct. 5 how the Emmy-winning “Succession” star brought his famously immersive acting method to the role of the Facebook and Meta co-founder.

“Jeremy Strong who gives a thunderous performance in the film is, yes, he’s an immersive actor,” Sorkin told Craig Melvin. “He showed up on the first day, I never heard him speak in his own voice. He only spoke, moved, behaved as Mark Zuckerberg, not just on the set, but when he went home too, 24 hours a day.”

A 2021 profile of Strong in the New Yorker broke down how he fully inhabited the role of Kendall Roy in “Succession,” which he called “identity diffusion,” rather than Method acting. The story describes Strong dressing like Roy in his regular life and staying in character to the point of concern from castmate Brian Cox.
Strong, 47, brought that same dedication to his portrayal of Zuckerberg, one of the most well-known tech moguls in the world.

“I know it seems weird, I know it seems perhaps even unnecessary, but the results speak for themselves,” Sorkin said. “It’s not silly, it’s not nonsense, it’s not like he doesn’t know we’re making a movie. He sees the crew and the cameras. This is his process, and I don’t think he knows any other way to do it.”
The new film, which hits theaters on Oct. 9, is the sequel to Sorkin’s Oscar-winning 2010 film “The Social Network” about Zuckerberg and the controversial origin of Facebook.

The movie tells the story of a 2021 leak by former Facebook employee and whistleblower Frances Haugen, played by Oscar winner Mikey Madison. She told the U.S. Senate in a 2021 hearing that it’s “clear that Facebook prioritizes profit over the well-being of children and all users” and said the company is “accountable to no one.”
Zuckerberg responded publicly by sharing an internal memo to staff that the company’s work has been mischaracterized.
Sorkin called the sequel “a whistleblower story” in the vein of iconic journalism films like “All the President’s Men,” “The Insider” and “Spotlight.”

“The film shouldn’t be political, unless you’re somebody who’s anti the truth,” Sorkin said. “The film is saying that the truth is important, and we’re not getting it. So unless you’re anti the truth, you shouldn’t find the film political, but yes, it’s going to be seen as political, primarily because of the final climactic sequence.”

title: Does Olivia Dean’s New Song Sound Like Bill Withers’ 1981 Hit ‘Just the Two of Us’? A New Lawsuit Says So
summary: How similar does Olivia Dean’s “I’ve Seen It” sound like Bill Withers’ Just the Two of Us?” Listen to the two songs.
story: Olivia Dean is facing allegations that one of her songs rips off a classic hit by R&B legend Bill Withers.

A new lawsuit claims the London-born Grammy winner, 27, steals a melody from Withers’ 1981 hit “Just the Two of Us” on “I’ve Seen It,” the closing track on her breakout hit album “The Art of Loving,” NBC News correspondent Joe Fryer reported Oct. 5 on TODAY.

The lawsuit was filed by Mattie Music Group, the publisher of Withers’ music catalog, against Dean’s music labels and publisher. Dean and her cowriters on “I’ve Seen It,” Bastian Langebaek and Max Wolfgang, are not directly named as defendants.

The lawsuit claims similarities between certain melodies in “I’ve Seen It” and “Just the Two of Us,” which Withers cowrote with William Salter and Ralph MacDonald and recorded with saxophonist Grover Washington Jr., are “obvious and inescapable.”

The lawsuit specifically compares the melody around the lyrics “I’ve heard it laced in every song and still words all come out wrong” in Dean’s song with the melody around the lyrics “I see the crystal raindrops fall and the beauty of it all…” in Withers’ song.
The lawsuit alleges the two songs’ shared musical features are “so striking,” and “did not result from coincidence, independent creation, or reliance on common musical elements.”

Dean, who won the Best New Artist award at the 2026 Grammys and is best known for the current pop hits “Man I Need” and “It’s So Easy (To Fall in Love),” spoke about being inspired by classic R&B music during an October 2025 visit to TODAY.
“I love songwriting and I love Motown and soul music, Aretha Franklin, music that makes you feel something and tells a story. I think its timeless,” Dean said.
The new lawsuit reignites a tricky debate that’s raged for decades in the music world: Where is the line drawn between artistic inspiration and theft?

Music journalist Tomás Mier told Fryer there’s been an uptick in music copyright lawsuits in recent years. “These estates are being a lot more particular with the sound similarities and going and being a little bit more litigious,” Mier said.

In 2015, the family of R&B legend Marvin Gaye won a landmark copyright infringement lawsuit when they successfully sued singer Robin Thicke and Pharrell Williams, arguing their 2013 hit “Blurred Lines” infringed upon the copyright of Gaye’s 1977 hit “Got to Give It Up.”
A federal court, and later an appeals court, agreed that “Blurred Lines” copied Gaye’s hit and ordered Thicke and Williams to pay nearly $5 million to Gaye’s estate in the case’s final ruling.

More recently, British singer Ed Sheeran triumphed against the family of one of Gaye’s co-songwriters in a legal battle that alleged Sheeran’s 2014 hit “Thinking Out Loud” copied elements of Gaye’s 1973 hit “Let’s Get It On.”
In May 2023, a Manhattan federal jury unanimously ruled that Sheeran and his co-writer on “Thinking Out Loud,” Amy Wadge, did not steal from Gaye on their song.
While the case was ongoing, Sheeran criticized such lawsuits in a video shared on social media.
Sheeran explained in his video that “coincidences” in songwriting are “bound to happen.”
“Its really damaging to the song writing industry,” Sheeran said. “There’s only so many notes and very few chords used in pop music.

title: Hoda Kotb Wipes Away Tears in an Emotional Tribute to the Saints’ ‘Domecoming’ Game 20 Years Ago
summary: Hoda Kotb looks back on the 20th anniversary of the Domecoming game in an emotional segment.
story: It’s been 20 years since that magical night, but just recalling the emotions of the New Orleans’ Saints first game back at the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina was enough to leave Hoda Kotb and Drew Brees wiping away tears.

Hoda and the legendary Saints quarterback recalled on TODAY Oct. 5 how a battered city in desperate need of hope and joy was focused on the Saints when they took the field in September 2006 for their first home game back in the Superdome.

“We took so much strength from our fans,” Brees said. “Truly, that night was a symbolic moment where we, as New Orleanians, had the opportunity to show the rest of the world, not only are we coming back, but we’re coming back stronger than ever.”
Their showdown against the visiting Atlanta Falcons came just over a year after Hurricane Katrina had devastated New Orleans in August 2025, laying waste to large swaths of the city.

The Superdome, a site of so much joy on Sundays, became a place of despair and horror as a shelter of last resort for displaced residents in the wake of the storm. The Saints didn’t play any games there in the 2005 season because it took 10 months of repairs to fix the damage to the iconic stadium.
Fans were able to put aside their hardships for a night when New Orleans celebrated its “Domecoming” game with a rousing 23-3 win that marked a milestone in the rebirth of the city.

Hoda, a diehard Saints fan and former news anchor in New Orleans, caught up with Brees as New Orleans gets set to mark the 20th anniversary of that night. Members of the 2006 team will be in attendance when the Saints play the Falcons on ESPN’s Monday Night Football Oct. 5 to commemorate the game.

Brees, now 47, had chosen to sign with New Orleans as a free agent ahead of the 2006 season despite the devastation that the franchise had suffered. He had suffered a potentially career-ending shoulder injury a year earlier while on the then-San Diego Chargers, so he saw New Orleans as a situation where both sides needed each other.

“Brittany and I looked at each other and said, ‘This is God’s calling in our life. Like, we belong here,’” Brees said about his wife. “This is about so much greater than just football. And how many opportunities do you get in your life to be a part of something like that?”
